pillars.title: Proximity ceiling of the map pack
pillars.section:
## T1 — The Proximity Ceiling of the Map Pack

**Bottom line:** The map pack is a proximity-capped surface. A single office ranks from one verified physical point, and pack visibility decays sharply with distance from that point — roughly a 5-mile average display radius ([Whitespark 2026, via SearchLab](https://searchlab.nl/en/statistics/local-seo-statistics-2026)). You cannot buy your way past that ceiling with a deeper website. You scale pack coverage only by adding staffed physical addresses ([Brandon Rollins](https://brandonrollins.com/p/how-to-rank-a-service-area-business-in-google)) — capex per market. Organic regional dominance has no such anchor. That asymmetry is the offer: the pack is a near-default proximity prize King Maker still delivers; organic is the engine that scales past one office.

**Proximity is a first-party, structural input — not a vendor theory.** Google names Distance as one of three primary local-ranking factors, alongside Relevance and Prominence ([Google Business support](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091)). In the expert-survey consensus, proximity is ranked the #1 Local Pack factor ([Whitespark LSRF](https://whitespark.ca/blog/7-local-search-ranking-factors-that-may-challenge-your-current-thinking/)) — directional, not a published coefficient, so we do not assert a precise percentage.

**Google tightened the radius by design.** The November–December 2021 "Vicinity" update — the biggest local algorithm change since 2017 — increased proximity weight and shrank the pack's radius of visibility, making it much harder for one location to rank outside its home city ([Sterling Sky](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/vicinity-algorithm-update/)). Whitespark ties a 360% jump in proximity-to-centroid importance directly to that radius reduction ([SearchLab Digital](https://searchlabdigital.com/blog/2023-lsrf/)). This is measured, current (2026), and not a stale 2021 artifact.

**The decay mechanism is measured.** Across 1,100 firms × 225 grid points each, pack rankings follow exponential decay with a sharp first-mile cliff — an average −8 positions in the first mile ([rankings.io data study](https://rankings.io/data-studies/proximity-data-study/)).

**The radius is density-dependent, so we promise a floor, not a mile number.** At max distance, the share of firms dropping out of the top 20 ranged from 27% (Pittsburgh) to 92% (Queens) — and some top-ranked firms saw no dip at all over 10 miles ([rankings.io](https://rankings.io/data-studies/proximity-data-study/)). The ~5–7mi figure is directional/modeled. The "FLOOR" is the conservative dense-market case; the "CEILING" is what organic prominence can dilate the bubble to.

**Rank is anchored to the verified address — not the service area.** Pack ranking is computed from the physical address used to verify the listing; the service-area setting is visual only and has zero ranking impact ([Sterling Sky](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/does-the-service-area-in-google-my-business-impact-ranking/)). A visible physical address is itself the 7th most influential pack factor across 8,186 businesses ([Sterling Sky 2025](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/what-gets-you-ranking-for-near-me-2025/)). So the pack is location-bound, not site-depth-bound — and structurally favors a real, located office.

**Scaling the pack costs capex; scaling organic costs content.** Because reach is anchored to a point, each new staffed physical address creates one new proximity bubble ([Brandon Rollins](https://brandonrollins.com/p/how-to-rank-a-service-area-business-in-google)). The pack is not capped at the company level — only per location. Concede that precisely: one office equals one capped bubble. The argument is the cost asymmetry, not a claim that the pack can never grow.

**The pack is valuable — just bounded — and the split is by intent.** In a controlled 5,500-tester study, organic out-clicked the pack (organic ~44–51% vs pack ~29–32%) ([BrightLocal](https://www.brightlocal.com/research/local-services-ads-click-study/)). But a strong skeptic source finds the pack drives more high-intent local leads and far more trust (~68% trust pack vs 27% organic) ([Spartan SEM](https://spartansem.com/map-pack-vs-organic-results-which-drives-more-leads/)). The defensible reconciliation is intent-segmented: the pack wins the urgent/emergency, ready-to-call slice (proximity-capped); organic wins the research, high-consideration, high-ticket-replacement slice and the wider geography. Home-services vertical corroboration matches this — near-me/LSA surfaces yield high-volume low-margin emergency jobs; organic and localized content yield the planned high-ticket replacements ([Diamond Group](https://www.diamond-group.co/blog/home-services-marketing-stack-for-more-profitable-jobs)).

**What NOT to oversell:** Do not promise a fixed mile radius or a measured per-location dollar cap (both are density-dependent inferences, not constants); do not call the pack "useless" or claim "organic beats the pack on leads" as a blanket — it wins the high-ticket/regional slice, the pack wins the urgent slice; never assert a precise proximity "%"; and exclude all PBN/link-scheme tactics outright.

loadBearing.claim: Google itself names Distance (proximity to the searcher) as one of three primary local-ranking factors, alongside Relevance and Prominence — proximity is a structural, first-party input to the pack, not a vendor theory.
loadBearing.stat: 1 of 3 core factors (Relevance, Distance, Prominence)
loadBearing.snippet: Distance: 'how far each business is from the customer who's searching' ... Prominence: 'how well-known a business is ... based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have.'
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: First-party Google documentation is the unassailable foundation of the whole pillar — it proves proximity is a Google-designed input, immunizing the offer against 'that's just an SEO theory' rebuttal. Goes on the foundational slide.

loadBearing.claim: Google's Nov–Dec 2021 'Vicinity' update increased proximity weight and shrank the pack's radius of visibility, making it much harder for one location to rank outside its home city.
loadBearing.stat: rolled out Nov 30–Dec 8, 2021; biggest local update since 2017
loadBearing.snippet: The update heavily increased the weight of proximity ... 'shrunk' the size of the map pack, making it much harder for businesses to rank in the 3-pack for locations outside their home city.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The keystone corroborator that the radius is a Google-IMPOSED cap, not an artifact of weak SEO. Independent (Sterling Sky), measured against a confirmed update. This is the claim that converts 'proximity matters' into 'the pack is structurally capped.'
loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: measured (confirmed algorithm update + observed ranking shifts)

loadBearing.claim: Pack rankings decay exponentially with distance with a sharp first-mile cliff — an average −8 ranking positions in the first mile across 1,100 firms × 225 grid points each.
loadBearing.stat: -8 positions/mile avg first-mile drop; n=1,100 firms, 225 grid points each
loadBearing.snippet: On average, the drop in ranking in the first mile is -8 positions ... [exponential decay] estimated constant lambda = 2.3
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The measured decay mechanism behind the effective-radius ceiling — the empirical 'how fast it falls off.' Reel-bound stat. Flagged as vendor-published but with disclosed independent data/methodology; cross-check the raw figure adversarially.

loadBearing.claim: Pack ranking is computed from the verified physical address, not the listed service area; the service-area setting is visual only and has zero ranking impact — so a single office's pack reach is anchored to one geographic point.
loadBearing.stat: service-area setting = zero ranking impact
loadBearing.snippet: 'the ranking is based on the address at which the business verified the listing. The only impact that the service area has is visual.'
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The structural root of the per-location revenue cap and the 'one office = one bubble' offer argument. Without this, a skeptic says 'just list a wider service area.' Anchors the capex-vs-content asymmetry that IS the offer.

loadBearing.claim: Organic out-clicks the pack in a controlled 5,500-tester study (organic ~44–51% vs pack ~29–32%), but the pack carries higher trust and wins the high-intent slice — so the split is by intent, not a blanket 'organic beats pack.'
loadBearing.stat: pack 28.8–32.3% vs organic 43.9–50.8% clicks (n=5,500); counter: pack ~68% trust vs 27% organic
loadBearing.snippet: Local Pack '28.8%' of clicks; Organic Results '43.9%'; when LSAs absent organic '50.8%' vs Local Pack '32.3%'. Study: '5,500 testers'.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The empirical spine of the 'organic is the engine, pack is a byproduct' frame — but paired with the Spartan SEM counter it forces the defensible INTENT-SEGMENTED framing instead of an over-claim. Most FTC-exposed claim in the pillar; must ship with the counter attached.

whatNotToOversell: Do not promise a fixed 'X-mile' pack radius — it is density-dependent (27% to 92% drop-out at max distance across cities); label ~5-7mi as directional/modeled and promise the conservative dense-market FLOOR.
Do not claim a measured per-location dollar revenue cap — it is a logical inference from address-anchored ranking + variable decay, never a published constant.
Do not assert a precise proximity weighting '%' (e.g. 55%) — the #1-factor ranking is from expert surveys (perceived/modeled weight), not a published causal coefficient.

Do not call the pack 'useless' or claim 'organic beats the pack on leads' as a blanket — organic wins the high-ticket/research slice and wider geography; the pack wins the urgent/emergency ready-to-call slice and carries higher trust (~68% vs 27%). Frame it intent-segmented.

Do not imply the pack can never grow at the company level — it scales by adding staffed physical addresses (capex). The offer argument is the cost asymmetry (capex per bubble vs content per market), not impossibility.
Exclude all PBN / link-scheme / gray-hat tactics explicitly — organic dominance is earned via on-page depth, content, reviews, and legitimate links only.
Treat the single-source '15% / declining proximity weight' figure as low-confidence — it conflicts with Whitespark's 2026 'proximity outweighs all other pack factors combined'; do not lean on it.
gaps: No primary source publishes a single defensible universal effective radius in miles; the ~5-7mi figure remains a directional synthesis of exponential-decay + density-variance data, not a measured constant. Treat as modeled.

No source quantifies a per-location DOLLAR revenue cap for pack-sourced leads; the cap is a sound logical inference (address-anchored ranking + finite within-radius population + 3 shared slots), not a measured figure — must be labeled as derived.
The proximity weight is directional (expert-survey/perceived), never a published causal % — the warm-context caution against asserting '55%' holds; no primary Whitespark table gives a clean number.

Roofing-specific decay data is thin: the cleanest per-mile decay study (rankings.io, -8 positions/mile) is a LAW-FIRM dataset. Mechanism (address-anchored proximity) is industry-agnostic, but a roofing-specific geo-grid would harden the claim — consider a Local Falcon SoLV roofing scan as own-data proof.
Exact post-Vicinity radius shrink is described qualitatively ('shrunk the pack', 'harder outside home city') but not given as a before/after mile delta in any primary source.

NO first-party Google doc puts a number on the proximity radius (miles) — Google only names Distance as a factor. Every mile figure is third-party/vendor-modeled. The ~5mi floor is defensible as a modeled consensus, never as a Google-published value. Promise the FLOOR, label it modeled.

The exact 'proximity is now ~15% down from 25-30%' decline figure has only a single weak (digitalharvest) source and conflicts with Whitespark's 'proximity outweighs all combined.' UNRESOLVED — do not cite the percentages; the directional 'radius can expand with engagement' mechanism is the safe claim.

No clean ROOFING-vertical or NC/Triangle MEASURED proximity-decay grid study was found (the two measured grid studies are personal-injury-lawyer and a mixed 1,100-sample). The decay mechanism transfers across verticals but a roofing-specific measured radius number remains a gap.

No source provides a hard dollar model proving a single proximity bubble caps revenue at a specific $ figure for roofing in a named metro. The cap is logically airtight (one address = one rankable point + finite in-radius population) but the $5-10M-needs-organic claim is an inference KM builds, not a cited measured figure. Frame as logic, not as a sourced statistic.

The BrightLocal 5,500-tester study (~29-32% pack vs ~44-51% organic) and the searchlab/Moz 2026 aggregation (~42% pack vs ~44% organic) DISAGREE on the pack's share magnitude. Both agree organic >= pack in click pool. Cite the directional finding (organic out-clicks or matches the pack) with a range, not a single point estimate.

counter.point: Individual-firm variance is large: 'Every law firm behaves differently. Some hold rankings for several miles, others drop out of the top 20 almost immediately.' A strong-SEO, high-prominence business can stretch its effective radius meaningfully beyond a weak one.
counter.soWhat: KM cannot promise a fixed mile number, but this actually SUPPORTS the offer: organic prominence (links, reviews, on-page) is exactly what dilates the radius — so the lever KM sells (organic dominance) is the same lever that buys extra pack reach. Promise the floor, project the ceiling.

counter.point: The pack still captures ~29-44% of local clicks and is the highest-intent surface within radius — calling it a non-scaling 'byproduct' risks underselling a genuinely valuable lead source for the home-market and emergency slice.
counter.soWhat: Frame the pack as the near-default proximity prize KM still delivers (and wins on ties), while organic regional dominance is the engine that scales past one office. Never say 'useless.'

counter.point: Multi-location is the sanctioned scaling path: real, staffed offices each create a new proximity bubble, and the biggest competitors already do this. A roofer COULD scale pack coverage by opening offices — pack isn't inherently capped at the company level, only at the per-location level.
counter.soWhat: Concede the per-LOCATION framing precisely: one office = capped. Scaling the pack requires capex (new staffed addresses); scaling organic requires content/links/authority — far cheaper per market. That cost asymmetry is the offer argument, not a claim that pack can never grow.

counter.point: No source publishes a single defensible 'X mile' radius or a per-location dollar revenue cap; the radius is density-dependent and the revenue cap is a logical inference, not a measured constant.
counter.soWhat: Label the ~5-7mi figure as directional/modeled and the revenue cap as a derived inference from address-anchored ranking + density-variable decay — never as a measured universal number. This keeps the FTC-exposed offer claim defensible.

counter.point: STRONGEST SKEPTIC SOURCE: the map pack, not organic, drives more local leads/conversions and carries far more trust. Spartan SEM: ~42% of local-intent clicks go to the pack vs ~27% to the top organic result; pack top-3 earn '126% more traffic and 93% more user actions' than those just outside it; and '68% of searchers trust Map Pack listings, compared to 27% for standard organic.' For high-intent immediate searches the pack is the stronger lead driver.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT over-claim 'organic beats the pack on leads' as a blanket. The defensible reconciliation is INTENT-SEGMENTED: the pack wins the urgent/emergency, ready-to-call slice (capped by proximity); organic wins the research/high-consideration, high-ticket replacement slice and the wider geography. KM should sell organic as the high-ticket + regional engine, not as 'more leads than the pack' overall.

counter.point: Proximity weight may be DECLINING, not fixed. A 2025 source claims proximity now contributes ~15% to rankings, down from 25-30% in 2020, and that strong user-behavior signals (clicks, calls, directions from 5 miles out) cause Google to EXPAND a location's effective radius over time.
counter.soWhat: Cuts both ways. It softens 'proximity is an immovable cap' (so don't promise an absolute mile ceiling) BUT it also strengthens KM's lever thesis: a deep, prominent site that drives engagement can dilate the bubble. Treat the specific 15%/25-30% figures as low-confidence (single non-primary source, conflicts with Whitespark's 'proximity #1, outweighs all combined') — cite the directional mechanism, not the exact percentages.

counter.point: Some sources put the pack's reach and click share HIGHER than round-1's controlled study: 'Map Pack captures nearly 50% of all clicks and appears in 93% of local searches,' and 'rural radius up to 15 miles.' Several roofing-agency pages call the pack 'the single most valuable digital real estate on the internet.'
counter.soWhat: These are mostly vendor-incentive (SEO agencies selling pack optimization) and inflate pack value. They contradict the controlled 5,500-tester BrightLocal study. Use them only to acknowledge the pack is genuinely valuable in-radius — never to concede the pack is the primary revenue path. The 15-mile rural figure does NOT rescue scale: rural = low population = low total lead volume, so a wide low-density radius still can't reach $5-10M.

counter.point: Multi-location agencies argue the pack CAN scale regionally — via 50+ geo-targeted location pages + a GBP/citation/heatmap profile per market — implying the ceiling is an execution problem, not a structural cap.
counter.soWhat: This actually CONFIRMS KM's thesis when read carefully: 'scaling the pack' still requires either real verified addresses (capex/footprint per bubble) OR the unique location-PAGE layer (which is the organic site KM builds). It is not the single office's pack radius scaling — it is the website's geo-page depth doing the regional work. Reframe, don't refute: the site is the regional engine; added pack bubbles need real offices.

This is the keystone corroborator that the radius is a Google-imposed cap, not an artifact of weak SEO.

'shrunk' the size of the map pack, making it much harder for businesses to rank in the 3-pack for locations outside their home city; businesses that previously ranked across multiple cities saw visibility reduced outside their immediate area.
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: measured (confirmed algorithm update + observed ranking shifts)

allClaims.claim: Pack rankings decay with distance following EXPONENTIAL decay with a sharp first-mile cliff: across 1,100 samples the average drop was -8 positions per mile, with the immediate first-mile drop ranging 5.3 to 11.8 positions. This is the measured radius-decay mechanism behind the ~5-7mi effective ceiling.
allClaims.stat: -8 positions/mile avg; 5.3–11.8 position first-mile drop; n=1,100
allClaims.snippet: 'immediately dropping anywhere from 5.3 to 11.8 positions' ... 'For all 1100 samples, the average drop was -8 positions.' ... 'rankings follow the law of exponential decay'

allClaims.claim: The effective radius is NOT a universal mile number — it varies sharply with population/competition density. In dense metros a single location falls out of the top 20 almost immediately; in lower-density metros it holds far longer. This is why KM must promise a FLOOR, not a fixed radius.
allClaims.stat: dense: Boston 81.5% / LA 82.3% / NYC 80.8% dropped from top 20; sparse: Columbus 28.5% / Pittsburgh 26.7%
allClaims.snippet: 'In Boston (81.5%), Los Angeles (82.3%), and New York City (80.8%), nearly every law firm has dropped out of the top 20' ... 'In cities like Columbus (28.5%) and Pittsburgh (26.7%), less than a third of firms had dropped out'

allClaims.claim: Pack ranking is computed from the VERIFIED PHYSICAL ADDRESS, not the listed service area — so a single office's pack reach is anchored to one geographic point. The service-area setting is visual only and does not extend rankings. This is the structural root of the per-location revenue cap.
allClaims.stat: service-area setting has zero ranking impact
allClaims.snippet: 'the ranking is based on the address at which the business verified the listing. The only impact that the service area has is visual.' ... 'Rankings are based on the address used to verify the listing.'

allClaims.claim: Because reach is anchored to a physical point, scaling pack coverage to a region requires ADDING physical locations (one proximity bubble each) — confirming the pack scales by capex/footprint, not by site depth. One office = one bubble = a hard revenue cap on pack-sourced leads.
allClaims.stat: each staffed physical address = one new proximity bubble; up to 20 service areas allowed but they don't rank
allClaims.snippet: 'Proximity to the searcher is the single strongest ranking signal in Google Maps' ... 'multiple Google Business Profile locations — each with a legitimate physical address, staffed and operational — each create their own ranking proximity bubble.'

allClaims.claim: The pack captures a large but NOT dominant share of local clicks — ~29-32% pack vs ~44-51% organic in a controlled 5,500-tester study. Organic OUT-CLICKS the pack. This is the empirical spine of KM's 'organic is the engine, pack is a byproduct' offer frame; corrects the inflated '60-90% pack' myth.
allClaims.stat: pack 28.8% (LSAs present) / 32.3% (absent); organic 43.9% / 50.8%; n=5,500
allClaims.snippet: Local Pack '28.8%' of clicks; Organic Results '43.9%'; when LSAs absent organic '50.8%' vs Local Pack '32.3%'. Study: '5,500 testers' across five SAB categories in San Francisco.

allClaims.claim: Google recommends a service area no larger than roughly a 2-hour drive — but that is a guideline ceiling on the SETTING, not a ranking radius. Combined with the address-anchored ranking finding, it underscores that listing a wide area does not buy wide pack visibility.
allClaims.stat: Google guidance: service area within ~2-hour drive of base
allClaims.snippet: 'Google recommends that your service area not extend much beyond a two hour drive from your business's physical base. However, the ranking is based on the address at which the business verified the listing, not the service area itself.'

allClaims.claim: A visible physical address is itself a measured top-10 pack factor (7th most influential, across 8,186 businesses / 200 cities) — independent confirmation that the pack rewards a real, located office and structurally disadvantages address-hiding service businesses. Reinforces that the pack is location-bound, not site-depth-bound.
allClaims.stat: visible address = 7th most influential pack factor; n=8,186 businesses / 200 cities
allClaims.snippet: Study of 8,186 businesses across 200 cities: 'a negative correlation between hiding your address and ranking well in the local pack' — 'Have a real office with a real address.' Visible address ranks as the 7th most influential factor.

allClaims.claim: Within the pack, click share is nearly flat across the three slots (#1 ~17.8%, #2 ~15.4%, #3 ~15.1%) — so the pack is the highest-intent surface WITHIN radius, but its total click pool is capped and shared three ways. The pack is valuable, not useless; it is just bounded.
allClaims.snippet: 'The #1 local pack result received 17.8% of click-throughs, followed by 15.4% for #2 and 15.1% for #3.' Pack ~44% of clicks vs organic ~29% in their aggregate framing.

allClaims.claim: Whitespark attributes a 360% jump in the importance of proximity-to-centroid directly to the post-Vicinity radius reduction — tying the modeled survey weight to the measured 2021 algorithm change, and confirming the radius tightened by Google design.

allClaims.snippet: 'Proximity of address to centroid ... saw signal importance increase 360% since the last LSRF, likely due to the reduction in the radius of visibility after the Vicinity update in late 2021.'
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: modeled (expert survey, tied to measured update)

allClaims.claim: A second independent measured proximity study (rankings.io, personal-injury vertical, distinct from the round-1 sample) confirms the exponential first-mile cliff: average -8 ranking positions in the first mile, exponential decay constant lambda approx 2.3, across 1,100 firms x 225 grid points per firm in the 50 largest US cities.
allClaims.stat: -8 positions average in first mile; exponential decay lambda~2.3; n=1,100 firms, 225 grid points each
allClaims.snippet: The ranking drops dramatically in the first mile; in all cities. On average, the drop in ranking in the first mile is -8 positions. ... [exponential decay] estimated constant lambda = 2.3

allClaims.claim: The effective radius is competition-density dependent and the variance is extreme: the share of firms dropping out of the top 20 at max distance ranged from 27% (Pittsburgh) to 92% (Queens), and some top-ranked firms saw no dip at all across a 10-mile radius. This is the measured basis for promising a FLOOR not a fixed mile number.

allClaims.snippet: The percentage of law firms that dropped out of the top 20 for each mile distance varies a lot between cities ... Some top-ranking firms do not even see a dip in the 10-mile radius

allClaims.claim: Whitespark's 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors data states an average ~5-mile radius in which Local Pack results are shown, and that proximity outweighs all other Local Pack factors combined. This is the cleanest single-number corroborator for the ~5mi effective-radius floor and confirms proximity dominance is current (2026), not a stale 2021 artifact.
allClaims.stat: ~5 mile average Local Pack display radius; proximity > all other pack factors combined
allClaims.snippet: 5 mi average radius in which Local Pack results are shown (Whitespark 2026) ... Proximity (distance to the searcher) is the #1 factor ... outweighs all other factors combined for the Local Pack

allClaims.claim: An independent home-services marketing source explicitly ties channel to job VALUE: Local Services Ads (and by extension the proximity-bound near-me surface) deliver high-volume low-margin EMERGENCY repair jobs, while organic search and localized content consistently produce the high-ticket, planned system/roof REPLACEMENTS. This is direct vertical corroboration of KM's spine that organic is the high-ticket engine and the proximity-capped pack is the emergency byproduct.
allClaims.stat: LSAs/near-me = high-volume low-margin emergency; organic+content = high-ticket planned replacements
allClaims.snippet: You may find that while LSAs deliver a high volume of low-margin emergency repair jobs, organic search and localized content consistently produce high-ticket, planned system replacements.

allClaims.claim: Google's own emphasis on proximity is NOT an absolute hard cap — it can be partially surmounted by superior relevance and prominence signals, expanding a single location's effective pack radius. The honest framing: proximity is the default heavy emphasis Google imposes, and organic/prominence depth is the lever that widens the bubble, but it cannot eliminate the distance bias. This prevents an FTC-exposed over-claim that the radius is immovable.
allClaims.stat: qualitative: prominence/relevance can outrank a physically-nearer competitor but does not eliminate distance bias
allClaims.snippet: If your business has built up stronger signals of relevance and prominence than competitors who are physically nearer to a searcher, you may succeed at outranking them ... your business will need to build up its signals of relevance and prominence to increase its chances of surmounting Google's emphasis on searcher-to-business distance.

allClaims.claim: The multi-location structural cap is corroborated by a roofing-vertical source: scaling pack coverage requires either Model A (each branch a separately VERIFIED street address + its own GBP) or Model B (one office as a service-area business), and when branches share structure 'Google can't clearly rank each location' (cannibalization). One office = one rankable point; regional pack coverage is bought with footprint, and location pages must each be unique to avoid conflict.
allClaims.stat: Model A = each branch own verified address+GBP; shared structure causes Google to not clearly rank each location
allClaims.snippet: Each location gets its own verified Google Business Profile with a street address. ... When all branches share the same SEO structure, Google can't clearly rank each location ... The One Primary Page Rule: Each city should have exactly one primary page targeting '[city] roofer' queries.

allClaims.claim: Recent (2026) click-share data corroborates round-1's 'organic out-clicks the pack' spine with fresh numbers: ~42% Local Pack vs ~44% other-organic, with pack slots near-flat (P1 17.8%, P2 13.6%, P3 10.4%) and the first organic result below the pack at 14.2%. The pack is the highest-intent surface but its total click pool is capped and shared three ways; organic remains the larger pool.
allClaims.stat: Local Pack ~42% vs other organic ~44%; pack P1/P2/P3 = 17.8/13.6/10.4%; first organic = 14.2%
allClaims.snippet: 42% of clicks go to the Local Pack ... Position 1 (Local Pack): 17.8% CTR ... Organic result 1 (below Local Pack): 14.2% CTR ... Other organic results: 44%

allClaims.claim: A general-market source frames the single-location ceiling in plain revenue terms usable in the pitch: a business 'might rank first when someone searches from one neighborhood and not appear at all two miles away,' meaning it wins a small radius while competitors own the neighborhoods where its highest-value customers actually live; capturing an entire region requires dedicated location pages for every market served.
allClaims.stat: rank #1 in one neighborhood, absent 2 miles away; region-wide visibility needs a location page per market
allClaims.snippet: Businesses that build dedicated location pages for every market they serve ... capture local search visibility across an entire region

pillars.title: Prominence dilates the pack radius (organic feeds the map)
pillars.section:
## T2 — Prominence dilates the pack radius (organic feeds the map)

**Bottom line.** Google names website links and reviews as inputs to "prominence," one of its three local-ranking factors ([support.google.com/business/answer/7091](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en)). A more prominent business can outrank a physically-closer competitor and surface across a wider radius ([searchengineland.com/guide/google-proximity-bias-in-local-search](https://searchengineland.com/guide/google-proximity-bias-in-local-search)). So building the deepest, most-linked site in the market is the engine that wins ORGANIC outright — and it feeds prominence, which is a stated pack input. That is the whole, defensible claim. It is not a promise that pages move pack rank by a measured amount.

**The mechanism, stated honestly.** Prominence is built from links + reviews + site authority; higher prominence widens the effective radius at which a business can rank ([searchengineland.com](https://searchengineland.com/guide/google-proximity-bias-in-local-search)). The magnitude is directional, not measured — published "5 miles vs 0.5 miles" figures are illustrative, not algorithmic readings ([eseospace.com](https://eseospace.com/blog/how-google-maps-rankings-actually/)). Promise the floor (authority widens reach around a real office); project the ceiling only as direction, never as miles-per-link.

**Where the payoff actually lands.** The link/authority lever pays off mostly in organic search, only softly in the pack. Whitespark's 2026 survey weights Link Signals at 24% for Local Organic vs just 8% for the Local Pack, and On-Page Signals at 33% organic vs 15% pack ([advicelocal.com/blog/2026-local-search-ranking-factors-maps-organic-ai](https://www.advicelocal.com/blog/2026-local-search-ranking-factors-maps-organic-ai/)). Sterling Sky's 8,186-business study found on-page content correlates only slightly with pack rank — review recency and a visible address dominated the pack ([sterlingsky.ca/what-gets-you-ranking-for-near-me-2025](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/what-gets-you-ranking-for-near-me-2025/)). Dedicated service pages rank #1 for Local Organic in the 2026 survey ([advicelocal.com](https://www.advicelocal.com/blog/2026-local-search-ranking-factors-maps-organic-ai/)). Translation: the site wins organic and only supports the pack.

**The cap is structural.** Proximity gates the pack. Pack results cluster in a tight radius — a 2:1 triangle that holds even in huge metros ([sterlingsky.ca/local-pack-clustering](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/local-pack-clustering-making-sense-of-googles-ranking-patterns/)). Hiding the address tanked rankings and in one case erased the pack for a keyword, and restoring it recovered them ([sterlingsky.ca/hiding-address-google-business-ranking](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/hiding-address-google-business-ranking/)). Distance is a hard input the site cannot override. A $5–10M organic footprint cannot be built on a 5-mile pack play.

**What NOT to oversell:** organic authority feeds prominence (a stated pack input) and widens reach around a real office — it does not move pack rank by a measured amount, and proximity still caps the pack.

loadBearing.claim: Google's own first-party definition of local-pack Prominence explicitly counts inbound website links and reviews as inputs — making web/organic authority a stated local-ranking factor.

If your business specializes in some goods, services, or amenities that are hard to find, you may find yourself ranking across a wider radius.

The number of reviews you've gotten this month matters more than your total number of reviews... a negative correlation between hiding your address and ranking well in the local pack.

whatNotToOversell: Do not claim a measured radius gain (e.g. miles per link). The radius-dilation mechanism is directional/mechanistic only; published 5mi-vs-0.5mi figures are illustrative, not algorithmic measurements.
Do not claim organic ranking CAUSES pack lift by X. The 88% organic-local 'correlation' is marketer belief (Moz survey), not algorithmic causation; pack and organic are modeled as separate systems.

Do not promise pack movement from website pages. Sterling Sky's 8,186-business study found on-page content correlates only slightly with the pack; the controllable pack levers are GBP + review recency, not the site.

Do not imply prominence overrides distance. Proximity is a hard structural gate — clustering holds in huge metros and hiding the address can erase the pack; prominence widens the radius around a REAL office, nothing more.
Do not sell a multi-million organic footprint as a pack play. Roofing/home-services is more distance-gated than average (~42% proximity weight); the pack is a proximity-capped byproduct.

Exclude all PBN / link-scheme / gray-hat. The link authority cited here is earned organic authority only. Ongoing client-managed off-page (GBP/review ops) is out of scope; only one-time shippable site authority is in scope.
Treat the link-weight figure as bounded, not headline: even maximal site/link authority addresses ~8% of pack weight (Whitespark 2026) — frame links as the ORGANIC engine, not a pack lever.
gaps: No source provides a MEASURED magnitude (e.g. 'X more links => Y additional miles of pack reach'). The radius-dilation claim is directional/mechanistic only — flag as such in any reel; do not invent a number.

Could not extract the exact Whitespark 2026 thematic weight TABLE (links % pack vs organic; on-page % pack vs organic) from a primary URL — the report page is JS/gated and the figure circulated by vendor blogs (e.g. 'proximity ~55%') did NOT trace to a primary Whitespark table, so it is intentionally NOT asserted here. Recommend buying/opening the full Whitespark PDF to lock the exact split before reel-binding.

The Joy Hawkins 'links matter more organically than in pack' quote came via search aggregation of Sterling Sky content, not a single confirmed article URL — confirm the exact source article/timestamp before quoting verbatim on camera.
The Moz '88% up from 65%' figure was captured via a vendor (Rio SEO) citing Moz's State of Local SEO; confirm against the primary Moz report for the exact year/wording.

No first-party Google statement was found that explicitly says 'your organic web ranking position' (as opposed to links/reviews) is a pack input — the verbatim Google doc names links + reviews only. The 'web results position' framing lives in the trade-interpretation layer (Search Engine Land), so attribute it there, not to Google.

No source provides a MEASURED miles-per-unit-of-authority figure for radius dilation — the 5mi-vs-0.5mi framing is illustrative/directional, not from a controlled study. The magnitude of radius expansion remains unquantified and should be promised as a floor (direction only), never a specific mile count.

No roofing- or NC/Triangle-specific dataset directly ties organic authority to pack-radius expansion; home-service proximity-dependence (~42%) is the closest vertical signal and it cuts AGAINST aggressive pack claims.

Could not verify the exact Whitespark 2026 weights on whitespark.ca's first-party page (nav-only on fetch); weights are confirmed via two independent secondary summaries (AdviceLocal, harmo.me) that agree — recommend a direct first-party capture before reel-binding the 24%/8% figure.

No causal/experimental evidence that improving a website CAUSES pack-radius expansion; all affirmative sources are correlational or practitioner-directional, while the strongest experimental local-SEO finding (address-hiding) shows PROXIMITY is causal and structural — the asymmetry favors the skeptic on the pack specifically.

counter.point: The single best independent measurement of what drives the pack (Sterling Sky, 8,186 businesses) found on-page/organic content correlates only SLIGHTLY; the dominant pack levers were review recency and a visible address — NOT website authority.
counter.soWhat: Promise the FLOOR: organic authority supports prominence directionally; do NOT claim a measured radius gain. The pack is won by proximity + review velocity, which is why we never sell the site as the pack-winner.

counter.point: Pack results cluster in a 'tight radius' / 2:1 triangle even in huge metros, and hiding the address can erase the pack entirely — proximity is a hard structural gate that prominence cannot remove.
counter.soWhat: Radius dilation is bounded. Frame it as 'prominence widens the effective radius around a REAL office,' never as ranking anywhere regardless of distance. Distance still caps the pack.

counter.point: Multiple authorities (BrightLocal, Media Captain) model pack and organic as SEPARATE systems with separate factor tables; the 88% 'correlation' figure is marketer BELIEF (Moz survey), not an algorithmic causal measurement.
counter.soWhat: Correlation between organic and local ≠ proof that organic CAUSES pack lift. Keep the claim at 'organic feeds prominence, a stated pack input' (defensible) rather than 'organic ranking lifts pack rank by X' (not measured).

counter.point: Link weight for the pack is small and DROPPING (~8% category, Whitespark/BrightLocal), and Joy Hawkins states link building 'doesn't directly impact local pack rankings.'
counter.soWhat: The link/authority mechanism pays off mostly in ORGANIC (the engine), with only a soft prominence assist to the pack. This is exactly the spine: organic dominance is the prize; the pack is a proximity-capped byproduct.

counter.point: Sterling Sky's 2025 study of 8,186 businesses across 200 cities found that adding 'near you'/location content to a page HELPED organic SEO but 'didn't move the needle at all for local pack rankings.' This is the strongest skeptic anchor: on-page/organic content is close to a non-factor for the PACK specifically.
counter.soWhat: Reinforces the honest ceiling — the site wins ORGANIC; it barely touches pack placement. King Maker must sell organic dominance and treat the pack as a proximity-capped byproduct, never promise pack movement from pages.

counter.point: Industry-segmented data shows HOME SERVICE businesses (the roofing vertical) rely on proximity even more heavily than average — proximity ~42% of the ranking weight for home services, vs reviews dominating dental/healthcare. Roofing pack placement is more distance-gated than most verticals.
counter.soWhat: The proximity cap is HARDER for roofing than the cross-vertical average. Pull organic-dominance forward in the roofing offer and band any pack claim conservatively; a $5-10M organic footprint cannot be a 5-mile pack play.

counter.point: Whitespark 2026 puts Link Signals at only 8% of the Local Pack weight and GBP at 32% — meaning even maximal website/link authority addresses a single-digit slice of pack ranking, while the controllable pack levers are GBP + reviews, not the site.
counter.soWhat: Quantifies the ceiling: building the best site in the market moves ~8% (links) + 15% (on-page) of pack weight at most, and on-page barely correlates per Sterling Sky. Promise organic; deliver GBP/reviews ops separately for the pack.

pillars.title: Link-absorption capacity (deep site vs thin site)
pillars.section:
## T3 — Link-Absorption Capacity: Why a Deep Site Converts Authority and a Thin Site Wastes It

**Bottom line.** A deep, siloed site has the structural surface area to convert link authority into organic rankings. A 5-page site does not. The mechanism is internal — fully shippable, fully controlled — and it is measured, not theorized. King Maker ships the absorptive structure: a 40–50+ URL spine, topical silos, and an internal-equity cascade. That is the one-time asset. It does not by itself earn the off-page links; it determines whether the links you do earn land as rankings or get wasted.

**Internal linking causally moves organic traffic — this is the core mechanism.** A controlled SEO split-test on a large retail site found that increasing internal linking produced a 25% uplift in organic traffic across category pages, with both the linked-to and linked-from page groups gaining 20%+ ([searchpilot.com](https://www.searchpilot.com/resources/case-studies/seo-split-test-lessons-increasing-internal-linking)). This is causal — control vs variant — not a correlation. A deep site has the pages to build this mesh; a thin site has nothing to link.

**The location-page case is directly relevant to a multi-city roofing spine.** A separate split-test adding links to nearby location pages produced a 7% organic uplift on those location pages ([searchpilot.com](https://www.searchpilot.com/resources/case-studies/seo-split-test-lessons-nearby-location-links)). A deep multi-location spine has the URLs to build a silo cascade like this; a 5-page site does not.

**Independent large-scale data quantifies the gap.** Across 324,522 websites, median monthly organic traffic rises from 18 clicks (sites under 10 pages) to 244,772 clicks (sites with 5,000+ pages) ([ahrefs.com](https://ahrefs.com/blog/average-organic-traffic-benchmarks/)). That is a roughly 13,600x median spread. Read it as directional, not as a promise — the same source is explicit that "a site that publishes 5,000 thin, near-duplicate pages won't see this growth; the traffic comes from quality content at scale, not page count for its own sake" ([ahrefs.com](https://ahrefs.com/blog/average-organic-traffic-benchmarks/)). The lever is *rankable* pages, not page count. King Maker's anti-doorway gate (real-job → page) is what keeps the spine on the right side of that line.

**There is a sweet spot per page — promise the floor, respect the ceiling.** A 23-million-internal-link study found URLs with 0–4 internal links averaged ~2 clicks while URLs with 40–44 internal links averaged ~4x that — after which the effect *reverses*: past ~45–50 internal links, traffic begins to decline ([zyppy.com](https://zyppy.com/seo/seo-study/)). A 5-page site cannot deliver even the low end of that internal-link volume to its money pages. A deep site can hit the productive band; the discipline is architecting toward the sweet spot, not stacking links infinitely.

**Deep-site link distribution is qualitatively safer, not just larger.** The same 23M-link study found internal-link anchor-text *variety* to be one of the strongest single correlates of search traffic — strong enough the researcher re-ran the data three times ([zyppy.com](https://zyppy.com/seo/seo-study/)). A site with many pages naturally generates diverse, contextual anchors into a target. A thin site funneling everything at one homepage money keyword is forced into anchor repetition — which is the pattern Google names as spam: its own policy lists "links with optimized anchor text" and "excessive link exchanges" as link-spam violations ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)).

**The risk to a thin site is wasted budget, not a guaranteed penalty.** Google's enforcement default against unnatural links is devaluation — the credit is neutralized, the gain turned off — with manual actions and Penguin-style demotions as the tail, not the base case (corroborated coverage of Google's December 2022 link spam update; treat the exact Google wording as reported, not first-party-verified here). So the honest framing is efficiency and safety: a deep site absorbs aggressive link investment across many URLs and anchors, so the budget lands as natural-looking diversity; a thin site wastes the same budget on a profile concentrated enough to get devalued, and carries the demotion tail-risk. A ~40–50+ URL spine gives roughly an order of magnitude more anchor-distribution headroom than a 5-page site — that is the claim, not "thin sites get penalized."

**Why this is the prize, not the pack.** In the map pack, site depth is a weak lever — proximity and review activity dominate, and a small well-optimized business can tie or win the pack on proximity alone. That does not weaken this pillar; it confirms the spine. The pack is proximity-capped (~5–7 mi); organic has no proximity cap and is where the 13,600x page-count gap lives ([ahrefs.com](https://ahrefs.com/blog/average-organic-traffic-benchmarks/)). Link-absorption capacity is the lever for *organic regional dominance* — the prize King Maker centers. The pack is a byproduct we deliver, never the headline.

**What NOT to oversell:** the clean causal evidence is for *internal* links (shippable, controlled) — earning the external links is ongoing and out of scope; the deep site makes future link investment *safe and efficient*, it does not guarantee links get earned or rankings get won; "deep" only works "deep + well-architected silo" (a sprawling unstructured page-dump leaks equity too); never state a dollar absorption figure or a page count as a rank guarantee; and never claim a thin competitor "gets penalized" — the defensible claim is devaluation/waste, not catastrophe.

loadBearing.claim: Increasing internal linking causally lifts organic traffic: a controlled split-test on a large retail site produced a 25% organic uplift across category pages, with both linked-to and linked-from page groups gaining 20%+. This is the core, shippable, controlled mechanism by which a deep site converts equity into rankings.
loadBearing.stat: 25% organic uplift; both page groups 20%+ (controlled split-test)
loadBearing.snippet: a 25% uplift to organic traffic across level two and level three category pages - an additional estimated 9,200 organic sessions a month... both the linked-from pages and the linked-to pages showed estimated uplifts in the 20%+ range. (Control vs variant, isolating internal linking from algorithm/seasonality.)
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the single causal proof that internal-link structure (the thing King Maker actually ships) moves organic traffic. It is the foundation of the whole pillar and the only piece of clean cause->effect evidence we fully control. Goes on the slide.

loadBearing.claim: Site page-count and organic traffic are exponentially correlated at independent scale: across 324,522 websites, median monthly organic traffic rises from 18 clicks (under 10 pages) to 244,772 (5,000+ pages) — but only for rankable pages; thin near-duplicate pages do not see this growth.
loadBearing.stat: Median monthly organic: 18 (under 10 pages) vs 244,772 (5,000+ pages), n=324,522; ~13,600x gap
loadBearing.snippet: 0-10 pages: median 18 (n=135,931); 5000+: median 244,772 (n=3,764). 'a site that publishes 5,000 thin, near-duplicate pages won't see this growth - the traffic comes from quality content at scale, not page count for its own sake.'
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: The strongest independent quantification of deep-vs-thin and the headline 'why organic, not the pack' stat. Must carry its own caveat (rankable pages, not page count) or it becomes a doorway-page promise. Directional, not a guarantee. Goes on the reel.

loadBearing.claim: Internal links convert to traffic up to a sweet spot, then reverse: a 23-million-internal-link study found URLs with 0-4 internal links averaged ~2 clicks vs ~4x for 40-44 links, after which traffic declines past ~45-50 links. A 5-page site cannot deliver even the low end of that internal-link volume to its money pages.
loadBearing.stat: 0-4 links ~2 clicks; 40-44 links ~4x; effect reverses past ~45-50 links (23M links, 1,800 sites)
loadBearing.snippet: URLs with 0-4 internal links averaged 2 clicks; 40-44 received ~4x more. 'After a URL receives about 45-50 internal links, the effect reverses. Google traffic begins to decline as the number of internal links rises.' (23M internal links across ~1,800 sites / ~520k URLs.)
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Anchors the floor/ceiling discipline (RANGES not point-promises) and proves a thin site is structurally incapable of feeding its money pages. Keeps us from overselling 'more is always better.' Goes on the slide as the deep-vs-thin proof.

loadBearing.claim: Google's own spam policy names 'links with optimized anchor text' and 'excessive link exchanges' as link-spam violations — so a thin site forced into repetitive money-keyword anchoring is funneling toward Google-defined spam, while a deep site's natural anchor variety is not.
loadBearing.stat: Google-named violations: optimized anchor text; excessive link exchanges
loadBearing.snippet: Link spam is the practice of creating links to or from a site primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings... links with optimized anchor text in articles, guest posts, or press releases... Excessive link exchanges ('Link to me and I'll link to you') or partner pages exclusively for the sake of cross-linking.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the PRIMARY (Google first-party) basis for the over-optimization risk, replacing vendor opinion. It is the defensible spine of the 'thin sites concentrate anchors into spam patterns' argument. FTC-safe because it is Google's own published definition.

loadBearing.claim: Google's enforcement default against unnatural links is devaluation (credit neutralized), not a guaranteed penalty — so a thin site's over-optimization most often WASTES the link budget rather than triggering collapse, with manual-action/Penguin demotion as the tail risk. Sell efficiency+safety, not a competitor penalty.
loadBearing.stat: Unnatural links neutralized / credit lost (devaluation), penalty is the tail not the base case
loadBearing.snippet: December 2022 link spam update used SpamBrain to neutralize the impact of unnatural links; widely reported as 'turning off' the credit rather than penalizing. NOTE: exact Google first-party wording could not be re-verified via WebFetch this pass (page returned blog index); corroborated via SE Roundtable / Authority Builders coverage — treat wording as reported, claim direction is sound.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the honesty guardrail for the whole pillar: it stops us from promising 'thin competitors get penalized' (FTC-exposed overclaim) and reframes to defensible efficiency/safety. Load-bearing precisely because it constrains the offer. Flag: exact Google wording not directly re-verified this pass.

whatNotToOversell: The clean causal evidence is for INTERNAL links (shippable, fully controlled). Earning EXTERNAL inbound links is ongoing and out of pillar scope — the deep site makes future link investment safe and efficient, it does not guarantee links get earned or rankings get won.

Never claim a thin competitor 'gets penalized.' Google's default is devaluation (credit neutralized / budget wasted); manual actions and Penguin demotions are the tail, not the base case. Sell efficiency and safety, not a guaranteed competitor penalty.

'Deep' only works as 'deep + well-architected silo.' A sprawling unstructured page-dump dilutes per-link equity (100 links = ~1/100 each) and leaks authority too. The value is the architecture, not raw page count.

The Ahrefs 13,600x page-count gap is directional/correlational and must always carry its own caveat: rankable pages only — thin near-duplicate pages do NOT see this growth. Stated bare, it becomes a doorway-page promise.
More internal links is not infinitely better — traffic reverses past ~45-50 internal links per URL. Promise the productive band (floor), not unbounded stacking.

Never state a dollar link-absorption figure (e.g. $5-10k/mo) or a specific page count as a ranking guarantee. The defensible claim is anchor-distribution HEADROOM (~10x a 5-page site), a mechanism, not a guaranteed outcome.
Exact safe-anchor percentages (exact-match <5-10%, disavow >30%) are practitioner-modeled and directional, not Google-confirmed — present as practitioner consensus, never as a Google rule.

In the map pack specifically, depth is a weak lever and a thin proximity-close competitor can tie or win. Do not claim the deep site wins the PACK on depth; it wins ORGANIC, which has no proximity cap. Keep the pack framed as a byproduct.
gaps: No primary Google source states an explicit 'safe anchor ratio' or 'link velocity threshold' — all specific percentages (5-10% exact-match, >30% flag, velocity spikes) are practitioner-modeled/directional. Treat as directional, never as a Google-confirmed line.

The '$5-10k/mo absorption' figure has no external source — it is an internal mechanism inference from anchor-distribution headroom (more URLs = more anchor variety). Frame as modeled, FLOOR = 'a deep site distributes link investment more safely than a thin one,' not a specific dollar capacity.

SearchPilot causal tests are on large enterprise/ecommerce/publisher sites, not small contractor/roofing sites — the direction transfers (internal links move organic) but the exact magnitudes (7-25%) are not measured in the roofing vertical.

Could not retrieve the Google Dec-2022 blog body verbatim via WebFetch (JS-rendered archive shell); the 'nullify the impact of unnatural links' wording is corroborated across multiple secondary sources and matches Google's known phrasing, but the exact one-line quote was confirmed via secondary coverage, not a direct read of the primary page text.

No clean study isolating 'thin site over-optimizes -> filtered' as a causal experiment — that mechanism is an inference chaining Google's spam policy + reasonable-surfer + anchor-distribution math; directionally sound but not a single measured result.

No CONTROLLED experiment isolating 'thin site vs deep site, same off-page budget' on identical local-service businesses exists publicly — the deep-vs-thin causal claim is assembled from (a) the SearchPilot internal-linking split-tests [round 1, causal], (b) the Ahrefs/Zyppy correlational page-count + internal-link data [round 2, large-n but correlational], and (c) the spam-velocity logic [directional]. Label the synthesis MODELED/DIRECTIONAL, not a measured single-study result.

No NC/Triangle or roofing-specific quantified case study (e.g. 'roofer added N city pages → X% organic lift') surfaced; roofing-vertical sources are prescriptive/agency (directional), not measured. The quantified backbone remains cross-vertical (Ahrefs, Zyppy, SearchPilot).

Could not independently re-verify the SearchPilot probability-of-positive-impact percentages on the aggregate page (the aggregate omits them); the round-1 per-test pages remain the source for those probabilities. The 7% nearby-location and 5% homepage-footer uplifts were re-confirmed on the aggregate page this round.

The Boshoff 'too-fast = ranking loss' finding is a LinkedIn/skool practitioner analysis, not a peer-reviewed or first-party study — treat the build-pace guardrail as directional. A primary Google statement on indexing-pace effects was not located.

counter.point: Google's enforcement default is DEVALUATION not penalty — SpamBrain 'turns off' the credit. So the thin-site 'spam-filter/velocity risk' is real but usually means lost gains, not a ranking collapse. Manual actions and Penguin-style demotions exist but are the tail, not the base case.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT promise 'thin sites get penalized.' Frame it as: a deep site SAFELY absorbs aggressive link investment because equity distributes across many URLs and anchors; a thin site WASTES the same budget (devalued) and carries elevated demotion tail-risk. Sell the efficiency + safety, not a guaranteed competitor penalty.

counter.point: The clean causal evidence (SearchPilot) is for INTERNAL links, which a site fully controls. External/inbound link acquisition — where over-optimization velocity risk actually lives — is largely an ONGOING off-page activity, out of pillar scope. The one-time shippable deliverable is the internal-mesh architecture + the rankable-URL inventory that makes future link investment safe.
counter.soWhat: Position T3 honestly as: King Maker ships the ABSORPTIVE STRUCTURE (deep silo + internal equity cascade + many anchor-able URLs). That is the one-time asset. It does not itself guarantee the off-page links get earned.

counter.point: Link COUNT -> rank is correlation; many 'factors' (incl. exact anchor ratios and the $5-10k/mo absorption figure) are practitioner-modeled, not Google-confirmed. The $5-10k absorption is a MECHANISM claim (a deep site has the surface area to spend it across silos without anchor concentration), not a guaranteed-ranking claim.
counter.soWhat: Never state a dollar figure as a rank guarantee. State: a 40-50+ URL spine gives ~10x the anchor-distribution headroom of a 5-page site, so a larger monthly link budget lands as natural-looking diversity instead of homepage anchor stuffing.

counter.point: More internal links also DILUTE per-link equity (100 links = 1/100 each) — a deep site is not automatically better; it must be ARCHITECTED (siloed, body-text contextual links, reasonable counts). A sprawling unstructured site can leak equity as badly as a thin one concentrates it.
counter.soWhat: The claim is 'deep + well-architected silo,' not 'deep' alone. The deliverable's value is the architecture (topical silos, contextual linking, controlled counts), which is exactly what King Maker bakes in vs a generic page dump.

counter.point: SKEPTIC'S STRONGEST POINT — in the MAP PACK specifically, site depth barely matters: 'a small, well-optimized local business can consistently outrank national chains' because Google weights proximity and review activity over domain size for local-intent queries; 'proximity wins every single time.' A thin 5-page site can win the pack on proximity alone.
counter.soWhat: This does NOT weaken the pillar — it confirms its SPINE. The pack is a proximity-capped byproduct where depth is a weak lever; the deep site's link-absorption capacity is the lever for ORGANIC regional dominance (the Ahrefs 13,600x page-count gap), which is exactly the prize King Maker centers. Frame: thin sites can occasionally tie in the proximity-bounded pack; they cannot compete in organic, which has no proximity cap and where page footprint exponentially correlates with traffic.

counter.point: Adding pages can HURT rankings if done too fast (Jonathan Boshoff, Ahrefs Top-Pages tooling): sites that increase pages too quickly lose rankings; the stated cause is 'outpacing the rate at which your site can acquire and distribute link juice (PageRank),' which dilutes existing pages.
counter.soWhat: A caveat on BUILD PACE, not a refutation of deep sites — and it actually reinforces the pillar's mechanism (PageRank is finite and must be distributed). The defensible posture: ship the deep spine but index/grow at a measured pace and back it with enough one-time off-page equity to feed the new URLs; do NOT dump hundreds of thin near-duplicate pages at once. This is the honesty guardrail against over-promising 'more pages = automatic traffic.'

counter.point: Page count alone is not causal — Ahrefs' own caveat: '5,000 thin, near-duplicate pages won't see this growth; the traffic comes from quality content at scale, not page count for its own sake.' And 96.55% of pages get zero Google traffic.
counter.soWhat: Bounds the claim correctly: link-absorption capacity is a CEILING the deep site can reach only if the pages are genuinely rankable (real service×city pages tied to real jobs — the anti-doorway gate). Promise the floor (a deep, quality, well-meshed site can absorb off-page equity a thin site cannot) and disclaim the doorway version (mass thin pages). This is the FTC-safe framing.

counter.point: Internal links have a saturation/inversion point (Zyppy): past ~45-50 internal links to a single URL, traffic declines.
counter.soWhat: Confirms RANGES-not-point-promises. There is a sweet spot, not 'more is always better.' Useful as proof of measured honesty in the pitch and as a build spec (mesh each money page to the tens, not hundreds, of internal links).

allClaims.claim: Internal-linking changes causally move organic traffic: a controlled SEO split-test on a large site found increased internal linking produced a 25% uplift in organic traffic across category pages, with both linked-to AND linked-from pages gaining 20%+. This is causal (split-test), not correlational, and is the core mechanism by which a deep site converts link equity into rankings.
allClaims.stat: 25% organic uplift; both page groups 20%+
allClaims.snippet: Not only was this test positive, but it was one of our most positive tests to date resulting in a 25% uplift to organic traffic across level two and level three category pages... Both page groups alone also had estimated uplifts in the 20%+ range, which means the increased internal linking also benefited the pages being linked from.

allClaims.claim: A deep site's MORE internal link sources is itself a ranking lever: a SearchPilot split-test adding related-article links showed a 95% probability of positive impact and a 16% uplift on the DONOR (linking-from) pages, with the combined groups showing a 90% probability of positive outcome and 11% uplift. More content = more pages that can both emit and absorb internal equity. (Honesty: recipient pages showed no detectable effect here, likely sample size.)
allClaims.stat: 16% uplift on donor pages (95% prob); 11% combined (90% prob)
allClaims.snippet: 95% chance of a positive impact on organic traffic, reporting a 16% uplift [donor pages]... No detectable impact on organic traffic [recipient pages]... 90% chance this change would result in a positive outcome with an 11% uplift [combined].

allClaims.claim: Internal links to NEARBY LOCATION pages causally lift organic traffic — directly relevant to a multi-city roofing site's silo cascade. A SearchPilot split-test adding links to nearby location pages produced a 7% organic uplift on the linked-to location pages. A deep multi-location spine has the URLs to build this mesh; a 5-page site does not.
allClaims.stat: 7% organic uplift on location pages
allClaims.snippet: This corresponded to a 7% uplift in organic traffic.

allClaims.claim: Google's own spam policy defines link spam as links created 'primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings' and explicitly names 'links with optimized anchor text' and 'excessive link exchanges' as violations. This is the PRIMARY-source basis for the over-optimization risk: aggressive exact-match anchoring is named spam by Google itself, not vendor opinion.
allClaims.stat: Google-named violations: optimized anchor text, excessive link exchanges
allClaims.snippet: Link spam is the practice of creating links to or from a site primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings... Advertorials or native advertising where payment is received for articles that include links that pass ranking credit, or links with optimized anchor text... Excessive link exchanges ('Link to me and I'll link to you') or partner pages exclusively for the sake of cross-linking.

allClaims.claim: Google's enforcement against unnatural links is primarily DEVALUATION, not penalty. The Dec 2022 link spam update used SpamBrain to 'nullify the impact of unnatural links' — ranking gains from spammy links are neutralized and the credit is lost, distinct from a manual penalty. This is the defensible framing: thin-site over-optimization most often costs the gain (devalued), with manual-action/Penguin demotion as the tail risk — NOT a guaranteed catastrophic penalty.
allClaims.stat: links neutralized/credit lost, not penalized (Dec 2022 update)
allClaims.snippet: Google reported it used SpamBrain to 'neutralize the impact of unnatural links'; widely reported: 'whatever effect they had on a website's rankings is now negated — this is different from penalizing... it only turns them off' (corroborated via SE Roundtable / Authority Builders coverage of the update).

allClaims.claim: Practitioner safe-anchor consensus: exact-match commercial anchors should stay under ~5-10% of the backlink profile; exceeding ~10% for a single phrase materially raises over-optimization risk. The bulk should be branded (40-60%), naked URLs (15-25%), generic/partial. A 5-page thin site funneling links to a homepage with the money keyword cannot hit this distribution — the limited URL set forces anchor concentration.
allClaims.stat: exact-match <5-10%; >10% per phrase = elevated risk
allClaims.snippet: keep exact match links down to less than 5-10%... [too many] can begin to look suspicious to Google's algorithm.

allClaims.claim: Internal links are a PageRank distribution system: link equity passes as a fraction per outbound link (a page with 10 links passes ~1/10 each; 100 links ~1/100), and equity decays with each click-hop from a high-authority source. A deep, siloed site routes equity down topical paths to many rankable targets; a thin site has nowhere to route it. Google has confirmed internal PageRank remains in the ranking system despite retiring the public toolbar metric.
allClaims.stat: ~1/N equity per outbound link; decays per hop
allClaims.snippet: a page with 10 internal links distributes roughly 1/10th of its equity per link, while a page with 100 internal links distributes 1/100th... Every page linked directly from the homepage receives more equity than pages accessible only through deeper navigation layers.

allClaims.claim: Google's 'reasonable surfer' model weights links by placement and click-probability: body-text contextual links carry the most weight, footer/sidebar links the least. This means a deep site's in-content topical silo links (high-weight) are both safer and more effective than a thin site's repeated nav/footer keyword links — the equity routing of a deep site is qualitatively superior, not just quantitatively larger.
allClaims.stat: body-text links weighted highest; footer/sidebar lowest
allClaims.snippet: Google's 'reasonable surfer' patent describes how link value varies based on placement, user behaviour, and click probability. The Reasonable Surfer model weights body-text links highest, footer and sidebar links lowest.

allClaims.claim: Unnatural-link risk is assessed RELATIONALLY across the whole profile — SpamBrain analyzes anchor-text distribution across all links to a target, the topical relevance of linking content, and historical velocity, not individual links in isolation. Practitioner disavow thresholds cited: exact-match commercial anchors >30% of profile, or >15-20% of referring domains showing network affiliation. A concentrated thin-site profile is exactly the relational pattern these systems flag.
allClaims.stat: risk flags: >30% exact-match anchors; >15-20% affiliated domains
allClaims.snippet: SpamBrain... analyses the relational patterns between the linking domain, the linked domain, the topic cluster of the linking content, the anchor text distribution across all links pointing to the target, and the historical behaviour of every domain in the network... exact-match commercial anchors account for more than 30% of the anchor profile.

allClaims.claim: Expanding internal link sources from a high-authority page (homepage footer) causally lifts the linked-to pages: a SearchPilot split-test found pages receiving links from an expanded homepage footer saw a ~5% organic uplift vs control. Confirms the 'more link targets fed by authority pages = measurable lift' mechanism that a deep site can exploit at scale and a thin site cannot.
allClaims.stat: ~5% organic uplift on footer-linked pages
allClaims.snippet: Pages that received links from an expanded homepage footer saw a 5% uplift in organic traffic compared to a control group.

allClaims.claim: Independent large-scale data shows site page-count and organic traffic are exponentially correlated: across 324,522 websites, median monthly organic traffic rises from 18 clicks for sites with under 10 pages to 244,772 for sites with 5,000+ pages — roughly a 13,600x median gap. A deep site has the rankable-page footprint to absorb authority into traffic; a thin 5-page site sits at the bottom bucket. This is the strongest independent quantification of the deep-vs-thin thesis found in round 2.
allClaims.stat: Median monthly organic traffic: 18 (under 10 pages) vs 244,772 (5,000+ pages), n=324,522 sites
allClaims.snippet: 0-10 pages: median 18 / mean 587 (n=135,931); 1000-5000: median 31,318; 5000+: median 244,772 (n=3,764). 'more pages only helps if they're pages worth ranking... A site that publishes 5,000 thin, near-duplicate pages won't see this growth—the traffic comes from quality content at scale, not page count for its own sake.'

allClaims.claim: A 23-million-internal-link study (Zyppy, independent) found the number of internal links a page receives causally tracks Google traffic up to a natural ceiling: URLs with 0-4 internal links averaged ~2 clicks while URLs with 40-44 internal links averaged ~8 clicks (4x), AFTER which the effect inverts — past ~45-50 internal links traffic begins to decline. This both proves a deep site's internal mesh converts equity into traffic AND establishes the FLOOR/CEILING discipline: there is a sweet-spot link count per page, not infinite stacking. A 5-page site cannot deliver even the low end of this internal-link volume to its money pages.
allClaims.stat: 0-4 internal links ≈ 2 clicks; 40-44 internal links ≈ 8 clicks (4x); effect reverses past ~45-50 links
allClaims.snippet: URLs with 0-4 internal links averaged 2 clicks; URLs with 40-44 received ~4x more. 'After a URL receives about 45-50 internal links, the effect reverses. Google traffic begins to decline as the number of internal links rises.'

allClaims.claim: The same 23M-link study found internal-link ANCHOR-TEXT VARIETY is one of the strongest single correlates of search traffic — strong enough the researcher re-ran the data three times. A deep site naturally generates diverse, contextual anchor text across many pages linking to a target; a thin site funneling links to a homepage is forced into repetitive anchors. This is the independent mechanism for why deep-site link distribution is qualitatively safer AND more effective, not merely larger.
allClaims.stat: Anchor-text variety = one of the strongest traffic correlates (re-run 3x); reliability degrades past ~25 variations
allClaims.snippet: 'The relationship between anchor text variety of internal links and Google search clicks was so strong that we ran the data three times.' Pages with at least one exact-match anchor received 'at least five times more traffic than pages without'; naked-URL anchors showed ~50% more traffic (no negative effect).

allClaims.claim: Google's 2024 Search API leak (independently analyzed) confirms PageRank is alive and plural inside the ranking system — multiple named components (RawPageRank, PageRank2, PageRank_NS 'nearest seed', FirstCoveragePageRank). This is primary-leak corroboration (stronger than round 1's toolbar-retirement inference) that the internal-link equity-routing mechanism a deep site exploits is real and current, plus Google's own Gary Illyes confirmed in 2017 PageRank was still in use after 18 years.
allClaims.stat: Multiple live PageRank variants in leaked API (RawPageRank, PageRank2, PageRank_NS, FirstCoveragePageRank); confirmed 2024
allClaims.snippet: 'Leaked Google search API documents reveal PageRank is still used internally' (Mar 27, 2024). 'A website's homepage PageRank can boost the authority of all its internal pages.' Illyes 2017: 'DYK that after 18 years we're still using PageRank (and 100s of other signals) in ranking?'

allClaims.claim: Authoritative trade source (Search Engine Land's link-velocity guide) confirms the spam-velocity mechanism that punishes thin-site over-concentration: a sudden jump from 10 to 400 backlinks in two days with no PR is 'a big red flag' that Google answers by devaluing links, demoting the page, or triggering manual review — and identical money-anchor clustering ('all 50 backlinks... use the anchor text best pet foods') 'looks scripted.' A thin site with few link targets is structurally forced toward both spike-concentration and anchor-repetition; a deep site spreads the same off-page budget across many URLs and many natural anchors, staying inside the natural envelope.
allClaims.stat: 10→400 links in 2 days = red flag → devalue/demote/manual review; identical-anchor clustering flagged
allClaims.snippet: 'a website goes from 10 backlinks to 400 in two days, without any newsworthy content or PR campaign. That's a big red flag.' Response: 'Devaluing the new links, Demoting the page, Triggering a manual review or action.' 'If all 50 backlinks to your article... use the anchor text best pet foods, it looks scripted.' 'Older, established websites can usually accelerate their link growth without consequences.'

allClaims.claim: Roofing-vertical corroboration: the 2025 roofing SEO playbook prescribes one-term-one-URL — a dedicated page per service AND per city — and warns that 'spreading multiple cities across a single page dilutes keyword focus and weakens map-pack potential.' This is direct vertical evidence that a roofer's many rankable service×city URLs (the deep-site spine) is the on-page requirement, and a thin few-page roofing site that crams cities onto one page is self-limiting. (Vendor/agency source — directional, but vertical-specific and consistent with the independent data above.)
allClaims.stat: One service / one city per URL; multi-city-on-one-page dilutes focus + weakens map pack
allClaims.snippet: Per the indexed snippet: 'dedicated service pages for each core offering... paired with location-specific pages for the cities you serve... This one-term-one-URL approach keeps topical relevance tight... Spreading multiple cities across a single page dilutes keyword focus and weakens map-pack potential.' (Note: 2025 'Diversity' local adjustment makes one site appear in BOTH pack and organic top-10 harder — reinforces choosing/owning the organic slot.)

allClaims.claim: WebFX (independent roofing-SEO guide) corroborates the structural prescription without vendor-incentive on the page-count claim itself: 'Create dedicated service pages for each core service' and 'Add location-specific pages for each city or region you serve,' with internal links listed as a core on-page element. Two independent roofing sources converging on the per-service + per-city page architecture strengthens the vertical applicability of the link-absorption thesis.
allClaims.stat: Dedicated page per service + per city/region; internal links a core on-page element
allClaims.snippet: 'Create dedicated service pages for each core service (e.g., roof replacement, storm damage repair).' 'Add location-specific pages for each city or region you serve.' Internal links named as an on-page SEO element to optimize.

pillars.title: Map-vs-organic ranking-factor weighting
pillars.section:
## T4 — Map-vs-Organic Ranking-Factor Weighting

**Bottom line: the two surfaces reward different mechanics, and only one scales with a deep site.** Local *organic* rank is won by on-page content and links — roughly 33% on-page + 24% links ≈ 57% of modeled weight ([Whitespark 2026 LSRF, via Sam Bretzmann](https://sambretzmann.com/2026-local-seo-ranking-factors-overview/)). The local *pack* is won by Google Business Profile and reviews — roughly 32% GBP + 20% reviews ≈ 52% ([same source](https://sambretzmann.com/2026-local-seo-ranking-factors-overview/)). A deep site plus one-time shippable off-page directly controls the levers that dominate organic. It barely touches the levers that dominate the pack. That asymmetry is the entire thesis: build for organic regional dominance; treat the pack as a proximity-capped byproduct.

**The full modeled splits.** Pack: GBP 32 / reviews 20 / on-page 15 / behavioral 9 / links 8 / citations 6 / personalization 6. Organic: on-page 33 / links 24 / behavioral 10 / personalization 8 / GBP 7 / citations 7 / reviews 6 ([AdviceLocal summary of Whitespark 2026](https://www.advicelocal.com/blog/2026-local-search-ranking-factors-maps-organic-ai/)). GBP is only ~7% of organic — the factor that owns the pack is nearly irrelevant to the prize that scales region-wide.

**These are modeled, not measured.** The percentages come from a Whitespark expert-opinion survey: ~47 leading local-search experts scoring 187 factors, aggregated by Darren Shaw ([methodology, via Sam Bretzmann](https://sambretzmann.com/2026-local-seo-ranking-factors-overview/)). Treat them as directional ranks (±several points), never as Google-certified weights. Confidence is high on the *direction* because two independent detailed summaries reproduce the pack column exactly ([Kyle Eggleston](https://www.kyleeggleston.com/blog/2026-local-seo-ranking-factors/)) and BrightLocal independently reproduces the pack-vs-organic split ([BrightLocal](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-local-algorithm-and-ranking-factors/)), and a different model (Moz LSRF) gives the same ordering — GBP ~36 / on-page ~16 / links ~13 for the pack ([Searchlab 2026, citing Moz](https://searchlab.nl/en/statistics/local-seo-statistics-2026)).

**The primary-source anchor under the model.** Google's local algorithm rests on three pillars — relevance, distance (proximity), and prominence ([BrightLocal](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-local-algorithm-and-ranking-factors/)). Proximity is a hard geographic cap unique to the pack; a website cannot move it. Prominence — backlinks, web references, content — is exactly what a deep site builds.
