pillars.title: The review-acquisition machine
pillars.section:
## PILLAR L5 — The Review-Acquisition Machine

**Bottom line.** Reviews are a top-tier organic-prominence lever, and the controllable edge inside them is VELOCITY, not total count. Google states plainly that "more reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking" ([support.google.com](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091?hl=en)). Independent testing shows ranking deteriorates measurably after roughly 18 days without a new review and recovers when inflow resumes ([sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/number-of-reviews-impact-ranking/)). The KM machine operationalizes a steady inflow — a one-time shippable funnel, then the client runs the recurring ask. We sell the velocity ENGINE, not a rank guarantee.

**What the machine is.** A `/review` deep-link funnel: one direct-to-Google write-review link (`https://search.google.com/local/writereview?placeid=...`) plus a QR code, fired post-job by SMS with email backup ([dreikon.de](https://www.dreikon.de/en/news/online-marketing-knowledge/link-to-google-reviews/)). Every one of these channels is explicitly sanctioned by Google — review link, QR code, follow-up text/email, in-bag card or window sign ([support.google.com](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474122)). The only constraints: no incentive, no pressure, no dictating content.

**One-time vs ongoing.** The funnel (deep link, QR asset, SMS/email templates, on-site widget + `aggregateRating` markup) is a ONE-TIME shippable build. The recurring ask itself — sending the post-job request after each job — is client-managed and out of scope here. We ship the rails; the client pulls the trigger.

**Equity vs citation.** This lever produces neither dofollow link equity nor a citation. Google reviews are a first-party prominence signal living on the GBP, plus on-site user-generated content for E-E-A-T/AI value — not a backlink. Frame it as prominence + trust + freshness, never as link equity.

**Compliance is a hard rail, not a tuning choice.** Review GATING — routing only happy customers to Google via a satisfaction pre-screen — violates Google policy ([support.google.com](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/7400114)) AND the FTC's final rule on consumer reviews, effective Oct 21, 2024 ([alston.com](https://www.alston.com/en/insights/publications/2024/10/ftc-issues-final-rule-on-fake-reviews-testimonials)). Penalties run to $53,088 per violation in 2026, and each suppressed review can count separately ([crowell.com](https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/keeping-it-real-ftc-targets-fake-reviews-in-first-consumer-review-rule)). Many off-the-shelf tools default to gating; the KM flow routes EVERYONE to the same unscreened write-review link. No sentiment fork.

**Sizing the prize (floor/ceiling).** Reviews carry roughly 20% of local-pack ranking weight per the Whitespark/BrightLocal expert survey — up from 16% in 2023 ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-local-algorithm-and-ranking-factors/)). That is a MODELED expert-survey weighting, not a published Google coefficient — label it as such on any slide. Floor: reviews are a confirmed prominence factor (Google's own words). Ceiling: ~20% of the pack algorithm and the 2nd-ranked AI-search-visibility factor, growing year over year. Recency specifically ranks as the 11th-most-influential single factor.

**Impact vs effort.** HIGH impact, LOW one-time effort. Approximate one-time cost: the funnel is a half-day to one-day build on top of the template (deep-link generation, QR asset, `/review` route, SMS/email copy, on-site widget + schema) — call it a single work-order block, not a separate line item. The recurring lift is the client's, and it's a 30-second SMS per job.

**On-site reviews — set the expectation up front.** A business marking up reviews about ITSELF (self-hosted or embedded widget) is INELIGIBLE for Google star rich results ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/review-snippet)). The on-site widget + `aggregateRating` is a content/E-E-A-T/AI/conversion asset — explicitly NOT a SERP gold-star play. Say this before the build, not after.

**What NOT to oversell:** Don't promise pack position from reviews alone (velocity is necessary, not sufficient — proximity and GBP primary category still gate the pack); don't promise SERP gold stars from on-site reviews; don't claim coached keywords in review text move rankings (Sterling Sky's isolated test showed keyword-seeded reviews did NOT lift — and actually saw the target term decline — [sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/does-the-text-of-a-google-review-affect-map-pack-rankings/)); and present the funnel multipliers (3-5x, 98% SMS open, 24-48h window) as DIRECTIONAL vendor benchmarks, never measured guarantees.

loadBearing.claim: Google's own first-party guidance states that more reviews and positive ratings help local ranking — the canonical primary source under the Prominence pillar.
loadBearing.stat: Verbatim Google: 'More reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking.'
loadBearing.snippet: Under 'Prominence': 'More reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking.' Prominence 'is also based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have.'
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the offer's core premise stated by Google itself — the strongest possible citation that reviews are a real ranking lever. Anchors every reel/pitch claim that the review machine drives organic prominence.
loadBearing.measured_or_modeled: directional (first-party platform statement, not a quantified weight)

loadBearing.claim: Review VELOCITY (consistent recency of new reviews) is a more impactful local-pack lever than a large static total — rankings deteriorate after ~18 days without a new review and recover when inflow resumes.
loadBearing.stat: Rankings 'fall off a cliff' after ~18 days / 3 weeks of no new reviews; recency > stagnant total
loadBearing.snippet: Consistent monthly reviews (recency) are more impactful than having a large, stagnant total. ... Rankings can 'fall off a cliff' if you stop receiving reviews for even three weeks; stay consistent.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the empirical justification for selling a VELOCITY machine rather than a one-time review push — it defines what the recurring client ask is FOR. The headline differentiator of the lever.

loadBearing.claim: Review gating (satisfaction pre-screen routing only happy customers to Google) violates both Google policy and the FTC's final rule (effective Oct 21, 2024), with civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation in 2026 — so the machine must route everyone to one unscreened write-review link.
loadBearing.stat: Gating = Google + FTC violation; up to $53,088/violation (2026, inflation-adjusted)
loadBearing.snippet: civil penalties of up to $53,088 per violation ... Forbids suppressing or selectively displaying reviews based on their negative sentiment or rating
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: FTC-exposure rail. The offer is reel/pitch-bound and legally exposed; promising or building a gating funnel is a federal-penalty liability. This claim defines the hard compliance boundary of the entire lever.

loadBearing.claim: Reviews carry roughly 20% of local-pack ranking weight (up from 16% in 2023) per the Whitespark/BrightLocal expert survey — a MODELED expert-survey weighting, not a published Google coefficient.
loadBearing.stat: Reviews ~20% of local-pack factors in 2026 (up from 16% in 2023); 2nd most important AI-search-visibility factor; recency = 11th-ranked factor
loadBearing.snippet: Reviews account for 20% of Local Pack/Maps ranking factors in the 2026 survey, up from 16% in 2023. Recency listed as 11th-most-important local-pack factor; reviews rank as the 2nd most important factor for AI search visibility at 16%.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the number that sizes the prize on a slide. It MUST be tagged as expert-survey/modeled every time it appears — asserting it as Google's literal weight is the cardinal sin for this lever.

loadBearing.claim: Self-hosted/embedded reviews marked up via the business's own schema are INELIGIBLE for Google star rich results — the on-site widget is a content/E-E-A-T/conversion asset, not a SERP-star play.
loadBearing.stat: Self-controlled reviews on own site = ineligible for star feature
loadBearing.snippet: If the entity that's being reviewed controls the reviews about itself, their pages that use LocalBusiness or any other type of Organization structured data are ineligible for star review feature. For example, a review about entity A is placed on the website of entity A, either directly in their structured data or through an embedded third-party widget.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Prevents the single most likely client disappointment — expecting gold stars in the SERP from the on-site widget. Sets the honest expectation before the build and keeps the offer from over-promising a SERP feature it can't deliver.

whatNotToOversell: Don't promise local-pack POSITION from reviews alone — velocity is necessary, not sufficient; proximity and GBP primary category still gate the pack (sterlingsky.ca).
Don't promise SERP gold stars from on-site/embedded reviews — self-controlled reviews are ineligible for the star rich result (developers.google.com).

Don't claim coached keywords in review text move rankings — Sterling Sky's isolated test showed keyword-seeded reviews did not lift, and the target term declined; correct floor is 'frictionless written reviews' since text>stars is real, but coached keywords don't rank and brush Google's ToS (sterlingsky.ca/does-the-text...).

Present funnel multipliers (3-5x from a direct link, ~98% SMS open rate, 24-48h window) as DIRECTIONAL vendor/Twilio-chain benchmarks, never measured guarantees — the floor is 'materially more reviews than verbal asks' (dialmycalls.com / dreikon.de).
Always tag the ~20% pack weight as a modeled expert-survey figure, never as Google's literal coefficient — algorithm weights are not published (brightlocal.com).

Never build or promise a gating/sentiment-fork funnel — it's a Google policy and FTC violation up to $53,088/violation; the flow routes everyone to one unscreened link (crowell.com / support.google.com).
Scope honestly: the funnel is one-time shippable; the recurring ask is client-managed and out of scope. Reviews are a prominence/trust signal, not link equity or a citation.
gaps: No independent (non-vendor) measured study isolating SMS-vs-email review-request CONVERSION specifically for home-service contractors; the 98%/3-5x figures are vendor/Twilio-chain directional benchmarks.

FTC penalty exact 2026 figure has two cited values in circulation ($51,744 original final-rule vs $53,088 inflation-adjusted) — both sourced here; confirm the current-year DOJ/FTC inflation-adjustment table before quoting a single number in a reel.
No primary Google doc quantifying how much (if any) on-site embedded reviews move ORGANIC rank vs pure conversion/E-E-A-T — the freshness/UGC benefit is directional, not measured.
Sterling Sky's 'Magic 10' and 18-day dormancy are from their observed case-study sample, not a published large-n controlled experiment; treat as strong directional, not universal law.

Did not separately confirm whether KM's specific Summit&Oak ReviewButton/GoogleReviewsWidget implementation uses a sentiment fork — must code-audit the actual /review + /reviews routes to certify no gating before claiming compliant.

No NC/Triangle/Raleigh-specific review-velocity or local-pack data surfaced — all geo-agnostic. If a Triangle-market claim is needed for the offer, it must be modeled from the national figures and labeled as such, not asserted as local fact.

The Federal Register .gov primary for the 2026 $53,088 FTC penalty figure blocks automated fetch (302 to an unblock/CAPTCHA page). The figure is corroborated across two independent law-firm sources (Crowell round 1; Venable here referencing the same adjustment) but the raw .gov citation could not be captured this pass — retrieve manually if a .gov-grade cite is required for FTC-exposed copy.

The third-party-review-diversity + AI-citation figures (Google 71% of reviews, 60% of AI citations to third parties) trace only to an agency aggregation page, not a primary BrightLocal/SearchAtlas study — confidence is low until traced to the originating dataset. Worth a dedicated chase before it becomes load-bearing in the offer.

No isolated, controlled experiment was found that quantifies the RANK delta from a specific monthly review cadence (e.g. '+N positions per X reviews/month') — the velocity evidence is directional/observational (case studies + large-n correlation), never a clean dose-response curve. Promise the mechanism, not a numeric rank lift.
The SMS ~98% open-rate stat (round 1) remains a Twilio/vendor-chain figure; no independent corroborator surfaced this pass to break the vendor-incentive flag.

counter.point: Google itself cautions reviews are 'only one piece of the puzzle' — Sterling Sky's own study notes a high review count does not guarantee ranking. Velocity is necessary, not sufficient; proximity and GBP primary-category still gate the pack.
counter.soWhat: Sell the review machine as a velocity ENGINE inside the organic system, not a standalone rank guarantee. Don't promise pack position from reviews alone.

counter.point: The headline conversion stats for the funnel mechanics (3-5x from a direct link, 98% SMS open rate, 24-48h window) come from vendor/agency blogs and a Twilio-cited chain — not independent studies. The DIRECTION is well-corroborated; the exact magnitudes are soft.
counter.soWhat: Promise the mechanism (direct link + SMS + timed post-job fire), present the multipliers as directional industry benchmarks, not measured guarantees. Floor = 'materially more reviews than verbal asks.'

counter.point: The ~20% pack weight for reviews is an EXPERT-SURVEY (Whitespark LSRF) — modeled opinion, not a measured coefficient from Google. Algorithm weights are not published.
counter.soWhat: Always tag the 20% as a modeled expert-survey figure when it appears in a reel/pitch; never assert it as Google's literal weight.

counter.point: Self-hosted/embedded reviews will NOT show star rich-results in the SERP (Google primary). A client expecting gold stars under their listing from the on-site widget will feel misled.
counter.soWhat: Frame the on-site review widget + aggregateRating as a content/E-E-A-T/AI signal and conversion/trust asset — explicitly NOT a SERP-star play. Set the expectation before the build, not after.

counter.point: Many off-the-shelf review tools default to a satisfaction pre-screen ('rate us 1-5; 4-5 go to Google, 1-3 go to a private form') — that IS gating and is now an FTC + Google violation. The machine must NOT replicate that pattern.
counter.soWhat: The KM /review flow routes EVERYONE to the same unscreened Google write-review link. No sentiment fork. This is a hard compliance rail, not a tuning choice.

counter.point: DIRECT CONTRADICTION of round 1's claim #13 (review TEXT/keywords help SEO). Sterling Sky's controlled case study seeded a Christmas-tree farm with 6 keyword-rich reviews ('Christmas trees', 'fresh trees') in the off-season and tracked rankings: keyword-stuffed reviews did NOT improve ranking — the target keyword actually DECLINED. Verbatim: 'adding keywords to reviews did not help this business' local pack ranking on Maps' and 'Don't coach your clients to include certain words in their reviews... this case study shows that it does not improve rankings.'
counter.soWhat: KM must NOT promise that prompting customers to name the service/city in the review text moves rankings. Reconciliation: a SEPARATE Sterling Sky finding shows reviews WITH text outrank ratings-only — so text-vs-no-text matters, but COACHED KEYWORDS do not (and coaching content also brushes Google's ToS). Correct offer language: 'we make it frictionless to leave a written review' (text > stars is real), NOT 'we get keyword-optimized reviews that rank you.' Promise the floor, drop the keyword-ranking claim.

counter.point: Correlation-not-causation caveat from the experts' own mouths: much of the review-weighting consensus is built on observed ranking movement, not isolated tests, and when individual variables (e.g. review keywords) ARE isolated they sometimes fail to reproduce. Industry sources explicitly warn 'something like keywords in reviews may definitely appear to help rankings, but when actually tested, we might see that they don't.'
counter.soWhat: The defensible posture: promise the MECHANISM and the FLOOR (a continuous-velocity machine that keeps fresh, real, written reviews flowing — which Google's own doc and two large studies support), never a deterministic rank outcome from any single review attribute. Label the 20% weight as modeled/expert-survey, not measured.

counter.point: Diminishing returns on early-review thresholds (extends round 1's 'Magic 10'): Sterling Sky's number-of-reviews study shows ranking gains from going 3→16 reviews, but the boost 'does not necessarily continue if you keep getting more reviews' — i.e. raw count saturates. The durable lever is VELOCITY/recency, not a perpetually rising total.
counter.soWhat: Reinforces, not weakens, the thesis — but disciplines the pitch: don't sell 'we'll get you 500 reviews.' Sell 'we install the cadence that keeps fresh reviews flowing,' since a stalled 412-review profile loses to a competitor with 11 in the last 30 days (the San Diego roofing anecdote, vendor-sourced/directional).

counter.point: Roofing-vertical 'case study' numbers in the wild are almost all vendor-marketing with NO sourcing (e.g. '52% more revenue,' '5 reviews/month minimum,' the San Diego 412-review anecdote, '4+ reviews/week outrank'). On direct inspection, the roofing review-marketing pages (Surefire Local, etc.) contain no quantified, sourced roofing-specific ranking data — only general principles dressed as benchmarks.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT cite roofing-specific review-velocity numbers as fact in reels/pitch — they're vendor-incentive and unsourced. Use the vertical-agnostic primary/independent sources (Google doc, Sterling Sky large-n, Whitespark, BrightLocal) and present roofing examples as directional/illustrative only.

allClaims.claim: Review VELOCITY (consistent recency of new reviews) is a more impactful local-pack lever than a large static total — Sterling Sky's case study tracked rankings 'falling off a cliff' when review inflow stopped for ~3 weeks (18-day dormancy), recovering when flow resumed. This is the empirical basis for the company-wide review MANDATE the KM machine operationalizes.
allClaims.stat: Rankings deteriorate measurably after ~18 days / 3 weeks without a new review; recency > stagnant total
allClaims.snippet: Consistent monthly reviews (recency) are more impactful than having a large, stagnant total. ... Rankings can 'fall off a cliff' if you stop receiving reviews for even three weeks; stay consistent.

allClaims.claim: There is a 'Magic 10' review threshold: moving from 9 to 10 Google reviews produced a small but noticeable Maps ranking increase for the main keyword, but 10→11 showed no further boost — the early reviews matter most, which is why the machine front-loads acquisition at launch.
allClaims.stat: 9→10 reviews = noticeable rank lift; 10→11 = no further lift (benefit plateaus)
allClaims.snippet: When businesses moved from 9 to 10 reviews, researchers observed 'a small but noticeable increase in their Maps ranking for the main keyword.' ... crossing from 10 to 11 reviews showed no similar boost

allClaims.claim: Review GATING — selectively soliciting reviews only from predicted-happy customers (satisfaction pre-screen) — is explicitly prohibited by Google's review policy, which states businesses must not discourage negative reviews or selectively solicit positive ones. The KM review ask MUST be universal/unscreened to stay compliant.
allClaims.stat: Gating = policy violation; ask must be unscreened
allClaims.snippet: Businesses should not discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews from customers. ... merchants should not require or pressure users to leave ratings or write reviews while on the premises, nor should they request that specific content be included.

allClaims.claim: The FTC's final Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (effective Oct 21, 2024) forbids suppressing or selectively displaying reviews by negative sentiment — making review gating a federal violation independent of any breach, carrying significant civil penalties. This is the legal floor under the unscreened-ask requirement.
allClaims.stat: Effective Oct 21, 2024; bans review suppression/selective display by sentiment
allClaims.snippet: the suppression of negative consumer reviews through inappropriate tactics ... The rule ... went into effect on October 21, 2024.

allClaims.claim: FTC fake-review-rule violations carry steep civil penalties — the original final-rule figure was $51,744 per violation, inflation-adjusted to $53,088 per violation for 2026. Each non-compliant review can count as a separate violation, so a gating SOP is a multiplied liability — promise the machine is built compliant, never promise gating.
allClaims.stat: $51,744/violation (2024) → $53,088/violation (2026, inflation-adjusted)
allClaims.snippet: civil penalties of up to $53,088 per violation ... Forbids suppressing or selectively displaying reviews based on their negative sentiment or rating

allClaims.claim: Self-serving aggregateRating markup (a business marking up reviews ABOUT ITSELF via LocalBusiness/Organization schema or an embedded Google/Facebook reviews widget on its own site) is INELIGIBLE for Google star rich results. The KM site can wire aggregateRating for content/AI/E-E-A-T value but must NOT promise gold review stars in the SERP from self-hosted reviews.
allClaims.stat: Self-controlled reviews on own site = ineligible for star feature
allClaims.snippet: If the entity that's being reviewed controls the reviews about itself, their pages that use LocalBusiness or any other type of Organization structured data are ineligible for star review feature. For example, a review about entity A is placed on the website of entity A, either directly in their structured data or through an embedded third-party widget (for example, Google Business reviews or Facebook reviews widget).

allClaims.claim: Even without star rich-results eligibility, embedding live reviews on the site is a legitimate ORGANIC asset: a steady inflow is fresh, keyword-rich user-generated content that signals an active/relevant page and feeds E-E-A-T (elevated by Google's 2024 core updates) — so the /review machine compounds organic dominance, not just the pack.
allClaims.stat: Reviews = fresh UGC + E-E-A-T signal (directional)
allClaims.snippet: A steady stream of new reviews—which is essentially user-generated content—signals to Google that your business is active and relevant ... E-E-A-T ... became increasingly important after Google's core algorithm updates in March 2024 ... Google will rank higher websites that show real people behind them by including reviews and testimonials.

allClaims.claim: Google explicitly SANCTIONS the exact channels the KM machine ships — a verified profile can generate a shareable review link and QR code, and businesses may follow up by email/text or place a 'Leave us a review' card/sign with a QR. The constraint is only: no incentive, no pressure, no content-direction. KM ships the rails; the client runs the ask.
allClaims.stat: Google-allowed: review link, QR code, follow-up email/text, in-bag card/window sign
allClaims.snippet: To leave reviews, you can ask customers to visit a Google link or scan a QR code. ... Offering incentives, like free or discounted goods or services, in exchange for customers to post reviews ... is considered fake & misleading content and is strictly prohibited.

allClaims.claim: The /review funnel ships a single direct-to-Google-write-review deep link (format https://search.google.com/local/writereview?placeid=PLACE_ID, or the g.page short link), removing the search-find-scroll friction. Businesses that share a direct link consistently collect markedly more reviews than verbal asks — the mechanism is the multiplier.

Businesses that share their review link consistently get 3 to 5 times more reviews than those that just 'ask' verbally. ... Print a QR code with your review link on invoices, business cards or flyers.

allClaims.claim: Post-job request timing is a primary lever: the conversion sweet spot is within 24-48 hours of job completion (or end-of-week for multi-day projects). The KM post-job flow should fire the review request inside this window to maximize capture.
allClaims.stat: Optimal review-request window = 24-48h post-completion
allClaims.snippet: Timing is the biggest lever in review collection. The sweet spot is 24 to 48 hours after delivery or service completion.

allClaims.claim: SMS is the highest-converting delivery channel for the review ask: ~98% open rate (vs email's far lower open rate), making text-with-a-link the primary post-job request mechanism, with email as the multi-touch backup. Flag: 98% is a Twilio-cited industry figure (vendor chain).
allClaims.stat: SMS ~98% open rate (Twilio-cited); SMS >> email for review requests
allClaims.snippet: compared to emails, SMS has 98% open rate, making it the single highest-converting review channel available

allClaims.claim: Reviews carry roughly 20% of the local-pack ranking weight (review signals: quantity, velocity, diversity) per the Whitespark Local Search Ranking Factors expert survey — a modeled/expert-survey weight, flagged as such. This sizes the prize: reviews are the #2 pack factor behind GBP, and velocity is the controllable edge.

allClaims.snippet: Review signals including quantity, velocity, and diversity are estimated to account for around 20% of Google's Local Pack ranking algorithm.

The machine's prompt copy should nudge specifics without dictating content (Google ToS line).

allClaims.snippet: Reviews containing actual text and keywords outperform star-only ratings significantly in SEO impact.

Round 1 sized the prize with a modeled expert-survey weight (~20%); this is Google saying it directly, the strongest possible citation for the offer's core premise.

The prize is growing, not shrinking, and within it recency ranks as the 11th-most-influential single factor and 'steady growth of reviews over time' is an explicitly listed factor.

Recency listed as 11th-most-important local-pack factor; 'Steady growth of reviews over time' listed as a factor; reviews rank as the 2nd most important factor for AI search visibility at 16%.

allClaims.claim: LARGE-N EMPIRICAL CORROBORATION of the velocity thesis: Sterling Sky's 8,186-business / 200-city 'near me' study found reviews-received-this-month matter more than total review count — directly corroborating round 1's velocity claim with a much larger sample than the single dental case study. Same study: a client generating 60+ reviews/month dominated until an 18-day pause, when rankings 'fell off a cliff,' while a competitor at a steady 15-45/month held position.

A dental client generating 60+ monthly reviews saw 'their rankings fell off a cliff' during an 18-day pause; higher average ratings 'tend to rank better' but not deterministically; reviews with actual text had a stronger impact than ratings-only.

allClaims.claim: COMPLIANCE RISK IS NOW ACTIVE, NOT THEORETICAL: in December 2025 the FTC took its FIRST enforcement step under the Consumer Review Rule, issuing warning letters to ten companies. Targeted conduct explicitly includes review SUPPRESSION — 'misrepresenting that displayed reviews reflect all or most consumer feedback while selectively suppressing unfavorable reviews,' which is exactly what review gating produces. The FTC is 'actively monitoring consumer complaints, online reviews, and company websites.' This is the hard legal floor under KM's unscreened-ask requirement: the machine must NEVER ship a satisfaction pre-screen.
allClaims.stat: Dec 2025: FTC warning letters to 10 companies; 6 prohibited behaviors enumerated, including review suppression/selective display.
allClaims.snippet: The FTC issued warning letters to ten companies for alleged deceptive review practices, identifying conduct including 'using legal threats or other coercive tactics to remove negative reviews or misrepresenting that displayed reviews reflect all or most consumer feedback while selectively suppressing unfavorable reviews.' 'The FTC is actively monitoring consumer complaints, online reviews, and company websites for potential Rule violations.'

allClaims.claim: Consumer-side recency demand has intensified in 2026, hardening the case for the velocity machine on the CONVERSION side (independent of ranking): BrightLocal's 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey finds 74% of consumers seek reviews written in the last three months, 32% look for reviews from the last two weeks (up from 20%), and 18% are only swayed by reviews from the last week. BrightLocal's takeaway: 'review collection should be continuous rather than occasional.'
allClaims.stat: 74% want reviews from last 3 months; 32% from last 2 weeks (up from 20%); 18% only swayed by last-week reviews.
allClaims.snippet: '74% of consumers seek reviews written in the last three months'; '32% look for reviews from the last two weeks (up from 20% previously)'; '18% are only swayed by reviews written within the last week.' 'For business owners, this means review collection should be continuous rather than occasional.'

allClaims.claim: REVIEW-DIVERSITY / THIRD-PARTY LEVER (new, AI-era): Google's share of all online reviews fell to 71% in 2026 (from 83% in 2025); Yelp ~6%, Facebook ~3%. More important for the AI-overview era: ~60% of AI citations point to third-party publishers (Yelp, Reddit, HomeGuide, Thumbtack) vs ~40% to the business's own site. Implication for KM: the one-time shippable rails should expose more than the single Google deep-link — a diversified review presence is now a competitive edge, not optional. Sized as directional (figures from a stat-aggregation page, not a primary study).
allClaims.stat: Google = 71% of reviews in 2026 (down from 83% in 2025); Yelp 6%, Facebook 3%; ~60% of AI citations to third-party publishers vs 40% to the business.
allClaims.snippet: 'Google hosted 71% of all online reviews in 2026, down from 83% in 2025, while Yelp accounts for 6% of reviews and Facebook 3%.' '60% of AI citations pointed to third-party publishers (Yelp, Reddit, HomeGuide, Thumbtack...), while only 40% cited the individual local businesses themselves.'
allClaims.measured_or_modeled: directional (aggregated, not traced to a primary source)

allClaims.claim: Whitespark independently corroborates the velocity/recency thesis and the 'no-saturation' framing: recency of reviews is the 11th-most-influential local-pack factor; 45% of reviewers pay most attention to recent reviews over any other factor; ~50% of consumers spend more time reading review content than a year ago. Miriam Ellis: reviews are 'the one stairway on this chart that is leading upwards' while link signals decline. The prescription matches the KM machine exactly: 'a steady, organized, repeatable process for acquiring reviews so that you always have recent content.'
allClaims.stat: Recency = 11th-ranked local-pack factor; 45% of reviewers weight recency above all; ~50% read more review content YoY.
allClaims.snippet: '45% of reviewers say that they pay the most attention to recent reviews vs. any other review factor'; 'nearly 50% of consumers say they're spending more time reading local business review content than they did a year ago'; reviews are 'the one stairway on this chart that is leading upwards into a sunny place of enlightenment.' Prescription: 'a steady, organized, repeatable process for acquiring reviews so that you always have recent content on your profiles.'

pillars.title: Other one-time levers
pillars.section:
## L6 — Other One-Time Levers

**Bottom line.** Beyond citations and the core GBP profile, a handful of one-time off-page assets are worth shipping — but only a few move the organic engine, and none of them produce a guaranteed link. We ship the *asset and the system*; the link, when it's a link at all, is *earned*. Everything here stays on the white-hat side of Google's published line. No PBNs, no link schemes, no scholarship links.

**Rank the levers by the master allocation.** The 2026 Whitespark Local Search Ranking Factors survey weights the local pack at GBP 32% / Reviews 20% / On-page 15% / Behavioral 9% / Links 8% / Citations 6% / Social 5% ([whitespark.ca](https://whitespark.ca/local-search-ranking-factors/)). That ordering — not intuition — decides what we build first and what we de-emphasize. It is an expert-opinion survey, so treat every weight as *modeled, directional*, never as a position-promise.

**The single highest-leverage one-time fix: the GBP primary category.** It's the #1 local-pack factor in the 2026 survey, and the wrong primary category is independently flagged by Whitespark as the #2 most common reason a business ranks poorly ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-local-algorithm-and-ranking-factors/), [whitespark.ca](https://whitespark.ca/local-search-ranking-factors/)). A GBP asset kit that nails the most-specific primary category plus ~4 secondaries (businesses with ~4 additional categories average map position 5.9) is the cheapest, highest-ROI deliverable we ship. One-time. Modeled, not measured — sell it as "we set the category Google judges you against correctly," not "+X positions."

**Manufacturer find-a-pro listings (roofing).** For a certified roofer, the GAF Master Elite / Owens Corning Platinum Preferred / CertainTeed SELECT ShingleMaster locators are credential-gated, high-authority, topically perfect directories the client is *already eligible for* ([gaf.com](https://www.gaf.com/en-us/roofing-contractors/verify)). True one-time setup, dofollow-class equity from a relevant high-authority root. **Conditional**: it requires an active certification. Uncertified clients get a "go certify, then we list you" recommendation — not a Day-1 deliverable.

**Reactive digital PR (HARO's successor).** We ship the *asset* — a pre-built expert bio, topic angles, pitch templates, and the monitoring setup on Featured.com / Qwoted / Connectively ([prezly.com](https://www.prezly.com/academy/the-best-haro-alternatives)). Reactive expert commentary is one of the three highest-performing white-hat digital-PR formats, and the resulting link is fully editorial — the journalist decides ([digitalapplied.com](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/link-building-2026-digital-pr-outreach-guide)). **Floor = the asset shipped + outreach running. Ceiling = an earned editorial link in a real publication.** We never guarantee a link or a count; that would be both undeliverable and a step toward the manipulation line.

**Local sponsorship / chamber / event listings.** Joining the chamber or sponsoring a local event yields a listing on their site — explicitly white-hat local link-building because it's geographically and topically relevant ([sterlingsky.ca](https://www.sterlingsky.ca/)). We ship the target list + outreach template. The link is earned via a real sponsorship, often nofollow, and priced as such — never bought as a ranking link with optimized anchor text.

**The photo/post kit is a CONVERSION asset, not a ranking lever.** The 2026 survey is explicit: geo-tagged photos have little ranking impact and Google-post quantity has none ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-local-algorithm-and-ranking-factors/)). Where photos pay off is engagement — Google's own first-party data: profiles with photos get +42% direction requests and +35% website clicks vs. none ([brightlocal.com](https://www.brightlocal.com/learn/google-business-profile/optimization/photos/)). We sell it on that honest footing. (The viral "100+ photos / +520% calls" figures are correlational and not first-party — we don't cite them.)

**The hard boundary — what we will not touch.** Google's spam policy defines link spam as creating links primarily to manipulate rankings, and explicitly lists buying/selling links, excessive exchanges, paid advertorials with optimized anchors, low-quality directories, and automated link creation ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)). PBNs are link schemes detected at network level; the penalty range runs from devaluation to manual action to complete removal from search — uninsurable against an organic-dominance offer. We also exclude scholarship links: Google cited a scholarship-link page in a real manual-action notice ([searchenginejournal.com](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/scholarship-links-google-penalty/408480/)). Treat it as a boundary, not a proven standalone trigger — the author himself notes it may have been incidental to paid links.

**The spine holds.** Every lever here is weighed against organic dominance, and the engine outweighs the pack. On-page is ~19% of controllable local factors and rising, with localized location pages + internal mesh central ([whitespark.ca](https://whitespark.ca/local-search-ranking-factors/)) — and it's the lever most fully in our control. Citations sit at the bottom (6%), so the aggregator/NAP kit ships as one-time *foundation hygiene*, never as a rank-mover.

**Equity vs. citation · one-time vs. ongoing · cost.** Primary-category + manufacturer listings = one-time, equity/relevance. Digital-PR + sponsorship = one-time asset, earned (often nofollow) link as upside. Citations = one-time foundation, no equity claim. Reviews are the strongest *controllable* lever (20%, up from 16% in 2023) but the **velocity is ongoing and the client's job** — out of one-time scope, noted not centered. Ballpark one-time build for the full off-page asset kit: low-four-figures of labor, not a recurring link spend.

**Impact-vs-effort read.** Primary category = highest impact / lowest effort — do first. Manufacturer listings = high relevance / low effort, gated on certification. Digital-PR asset = high ceiling / medium effort / unguaranteed outcome. Sponsorship = modest, durable, low effort. Photo kit = conversion impact, not ranking. Citations = low ranking impact, but cheap and foundational.

**What NOT to oversell:** the LSRF weights are a modeled practitioner survey, not a causal study; earned links (PR/sponsorship/chamber) are never a guaranteed count and often nofollow; manufacturer listings require a real certification; photos/posts are conversion not ranking; citations are 6% — ship as hygiene, not a rank-mover; scholarship links are an exclusion boundary, not a proven penalty mechanism.

loadBearing.claim: GBP primary category is the single highest-leverage one-time off-page fix — the #1 local-pack ranking factor in the 2026 LSRF survey and independently the #2 most common cause of poor ranking when set wrong.
loadBearing.stat: Primary GBP category = #1 local-pack factor; wrong primary category = #2 most common cause of poor local ranking; ~4 additional categories → avg map position 5.9
loadBearing.snippet: Primary GBP category is listed as the top local pack ranking factor... businesses using four additional categories within their GBPs have the highest average map ranking of 5.9.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the headline one-time deliverable in the off-page kit — cheapest, highest ROI. It anchors the offer's claim that the GBP asset kit moves rankings, so it must be cited and labeled modeled.

loadBearing.claim: Google's published spam policy defines and prohibits link schemes (bought/sold links, exchanges, paid advertorials, automated links); PBNs are detected at network level with penalties up to complete removal from search. King Maker excludes them entirely.
loadBearing.stat: Penalty range: link devaluation → manual action → complete removal from search results
loadBearing.snippet: Link spam is the practice of creating links to or from a site primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings... Exchanging money, goods, or services for links... Using automated programs or services to create links to your site.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the FTC-exposure boundary — the explicit no-PBN/no-link-scheme line the offer must stand behind. First-party Google source; defines what we will NOT do.

loadBearing.claim: Reactive digital PR is shippable as a ONE-TIME ASSET (expert bio + angles + pitch templates + monitoring on the active HARO-successor platforms); the resulting link is fully editorial and earned, never guaranteed.
loadBearing.stat: HARO closed Dec 9 2024, relaunched under Featured.com Apr 22 2025; reactive expert commentary is one of the three top white-hat digital-PR formats
loadBearing.snippet: The three highest-performing digital PR formats are: original data studies, expert reactive commentary (newsjacking), and free tools or calculators... a well-timed expert quote often earns more links than a planned campaign.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the high-ceiling lever on a slide; it must be framed as floor=asset / ceiling=earned-link or it becomes an undeliverable link-count promise.

loadBearing.claim: GBP photos/posts do NOT move local-pack ranking per the 2026 survey — they are a CONVERSION lever. Google's first-party data: profiles with photos get +42% direction requests and +35% website clicks vs none.
loadBearing.stat: Geo-tagged photos: little ranking impact; post quantity: no ranking influence. Photos: +42% direction requests, +35% website clicks (Google first-party)
loadBearing.snippet: Businesses with photos receive 42% more requests for driving directions and 35% more clicks through to their websites than businesses that don't have photos.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: Directly prevents the overclaim trap — bundling photos as a ranking lever is the kind of false confidence the FTC-exposed offer must avoid. The honest reframe (conversion, with Google's own numbers) is load-bearing for defensibility.

loadBearing.claim: The 2026 LSRF master allocation ranks every off-page lever: GBP 32% / Reviews 20% / On-page 15% / Behavioral 9% / Links 8% / Citations 6% / Social 5% — confirming citations are the smallest classic factor and GBP+reviews dominate. It is a modeled expert survey.
loadBearing.stat: Local pack 2026: GBP 32%, Reviews 20%, On-page 15%, Behavioral 9%, Links 8%, Citations 6%, Social 5%
loadBearing.snippet: On-page SEO accounts for approximately 19% of controllable ranking factors... local pages, localized content, and strong internal linking central to local success.
loadBearing.whyLoadBearing: This is the allocation that ranks/justifies the whole lever stack in the offer. It also keeps the spine honest — citations at 6% means we never sell the NAP kit as a rank-mover. Must be labeled modeled/survey.

whatNotToOversell: The LSRF weights (primary category #1, reviews 20%, on-page 19%, citations 6%) are a modeled expert-opinion survey, not a measured causal study — say 'modeled from the leading practitioner survey,' never 'proven to move you X positions.'

Earned-link levers (digital PR, sponsorship, chamber) cannot be guaranteed — the journalist/org decides, and many such links are nofollow or devalued. Promise the asset/system, link acquisition as upside; never a backlink count.

Manufacturer find-a-pro listings (GAF Master Elite, OC Platinum, CertainTeed SELECT) require an active certification the client may not hold — gate to certified clients; otherwise it's a 'go certify' recommendation, not a Day-1 deliverable.

GBP photos and Google Posts do NOT move pack ranking per the 2026 survey — sell them as conversion/freshness assets on Google's own +42%/+35% engagement data, explicitly not as a ranking lever. Do not cite the viral 100+ photos / +520% calls figures (correlational, not first-party).
Citations are only 6% of local-pack weight and have declined every recent year — ship the aggregator/NAP kit as one-time foundation hygiene, never centered or sold as a rank-mover.

The scholarship-link penalty is a single documented manual action the author flags as possibly incidental to paid links — use it only to justify EXCLUDING scholarship links (a boundary), not as a claim that scholarship links alone reliably trigger penalties.

No PBNs, link farms, link exchanges, paid advertorials with optimized anchors, or automated link creation — these are Google-defined link schemes with penalties up to full de-indexation; the offer must stay behind that published line.
gaps: No independent CAUSAL study quantifying the ranking lift from fixing a primary category in roofing specifically — only the practitioner-survey ordinal ranking and the 'position 5.9 with 4 categories' correlational figure.

No first-party data on what share of HARO/Featured pitches in the home-services/roofing vertical actually convert to a published, followed editorial link — the link-acquisition rate (the CEILING) is unquantified.

Manufacturer find-a-pro directories were confirmed to exist and be credential-gated, but their actual Domain Authority / link-equity pass (the WARM-CONTEXT 'DA ~60-80' claim) was not re-verified against a primary DA source this pass — carry it as directional.
No quantification of how much a single chamber/sponsorship link moves organic vs pack — only the qualitative 'valuable, white-hat' framing from Sterling Sky.
The '+42%/+35% photos' figure is Google first-party but undated; whether it still reflects current GBP behavior (vs older GMB) is unconfirmed.

No NC/Triangle-specific or roofing-specific MEASURED lift figure for any single one-time off-page lever (e.g. dollar/rank delta from a GAF directory link or NRCA listing) — all vertical evidence is practitioner-directional, not measured. The defensible move is to promise the ASSET and the relevance, never a rank delta.

The widely-circulated NAP-impact stats from this round's broad search ('40% more likely to appear in local pack', '23% more likely in 3-Pack', '17% improvement in 90 days') trace only to low-authority vendor/AI-content blogs (verlua, replywiseai) with no locatable primary study — deliberately EXCLUDED as uncorroborated/likely-fabricated. Do not cite these numbers.

Could not retrieve a clean primary snippet for John Mueller's 'size doesn't matter' paid-link quote (seroundtable 403'd); the exclusion is already authoritatively covered by Google's own spam-policy page from round 1, so this is non-blocking.

The reactive-PR / journalist-query lever (Featured/Qwoted/Connectively, HARO's successors) ranks #6 in the Footbridge list and was covered in round 1; no STRONGER measured corroborator found this pass — it remains a high-ceiling/earned (asset-not-guarantee) lever.

counter.point: The LSRF survey numbers (primary category #1, reviews 20%, on-page 19%) are an EXPERT-OPINION SURVEY, not a measured causal study — they are practitioner consensus, modeled not measured. Treat every weight as directional, never as a guaranteed lever.
counter.soWhat: In the offer, label these 'modeled from the industry's leading practitioner survey,' never 'proven to move you X positions.' Promise the asset shipped, not a ranking outcome.

counter.point: Earned-link levers (HARO/digital PR, sponsorship, chamber) cannot be guaranteed — the journalist or organization decides whether to link, and many sponsorship links are nofollow or get devalued. The deliverable is the ASSET/SYSTEM, not the link.
counter.soWhat: Price and promise these as 'we build and run the outreach asset,' with link acquisition as upside. Guaranteeing 'X backlinks' here would be both undeliverable and edges toward the manipulation line.

counter.point: Manufacturer find-a-pro listings require an active certification the client may not hold (Master Elite etc. are training/insurance-gated), so this lever is conditional on the client's real-world credentials — it's not universally shippable.
counter.soWhat: Gate this lever in the offer to certified clients; for uncertified ones it becomes a 'go get certified, then we list you' recommendation, not a Day-1 deliverable.

counter.point: GBP photos/posts have a strong intuitive appeal as 'optimization' but the 2026 survey says they do NOT move pack ranking — only conversion/engagement. Bundling them as a 'ranking' lever is the kind of overclaim the FTC-exposed offer must avoid.
counter.soWhat: Sell the photo/post kit honestly as a conversion + freshness asset (Google's own 42%/35% engagement data), explicitly not as a ranking lever.

counter.point: The scholarship-penalty case is a single documented manual action where the cited author himself flags the scholarship link may have been incidental to paid links — it is a boundary signal, not a proven standalone-penalty mechanism.
counter.soWhat: Use it correctly: as justification for EXCLUDING scholarship links (the boundary), not as a claim that scholarship links alone reliably trigger penalties.

counter.point: CITATIONS HAVE COLLAPSED IN WEIGHT — a skeptic's strongest card against any citation-heavy off-page kit. In the 2026 Whitespark survey citations are only 6% of local-pack weight (down from a historically dominant position; on-page is 15%, reviews 20%, GBP 32%). Citation-building has decreased in relative importance every recent year as Google relies less on third-party data.
counter.soWhat: Do NOT center or oversell a citation/aggregator/NAP kit as a ranking lever — sell it as a one-time FOUNDATION/hygiene asset (correctness propagates, supports trust + AI visibility) while pointing the offer's weight at the engine: organic on-page depth, GBP, reviews. Overstating citations is the defensibility miss. The aggregator submission is still worth shipping (it's cheap, one-time, foundational), just priced as floor-hygiene not as a rank-mover.

counter.point: Sterling Sky's INDEPENDENT 8,186-business / 200-city 'near me' study (2025) found ranking is driven by review RECENCY (reviews gotten THIS MONTH > total review count — a client paused reviews 18 days and rankings dropped), address visibility, and review TEXT — not by citation volume or one-time link kits. Photo value is industry-dependent (helps restaurants/salons, little for garage-door/roofing-type firms).
counter.soWhat: Reinforces that the highest-yield CLIENT-controllable lever is ongoing review velocity (out of one-time scope) — so a one-time off-page kit cannot be sold as the thing that 'wins' on its own. The shippable one-time piece is the review-SYSTEM + response-template asset; the velocity is the client's job. Honesty: a one-time off-page kit moves the foundation, the engine is organic depth + sustained reviews. Photos are a conversion lever for roofing, not a ranking lever.

counter.point: Google (via John Mueller, reaffirmed through the 2025 link-spam update) holds that buying/selling links to pass PageRank is a violation REGARDLESS of site size, and now expects paid/sponsored links to carry rel=sponsored/nofollow; SpamBrain increasingly just NEUTRALIZES manipulative links (ranking drop, no manual action) rather than penalizing. Any 'link package' that buys placement with optimized anchors is on the wrong side of this line.
counter.soWhat: Hard exclusion boundary for King Maker's offer: the one-time link levers must all be EARNED (credential-gated manufacturer dirs, real sponsorships/memberships, editorial best-of placements) — never bought-for-rank with optimized anchors, never PBNs, never link packages. Best case a bought link is silently devalued (wasted spend); worst case the whole profile is discounted. Promise earned assets, not link counts.

allClaims.claim: Google's own spam policy defines link spam as creating links primarily to manipulate rankings, and explicitly lists buying/selling links, excessive link exchanges, paid advertorials/native ads with optimized anchor text, low-quality directory/bookmark links, and automated link creation as violations. This is the explicit NO-PBN / NO-link-scheme penalty line King Maker must stay behind.
allClaims.stat: Verbatim: 'Link spam is the practice of creating links to or from a site primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings.'
allClaims.snippet: Link spam is the practice of creating links to or from a site primarily for the purpose of manipulating search rankings. ... Exchanging money, goods, or services for links ... Excessive link exchanges ('Link to me and I'll link to you') or partner pages exclusively for the sake of cross-linking ... Advertorials or native advertising where payment is received for articles that include links that pass ranking credit, or links with optimized anchor text ... Low-quality directory or bookmark site links ... Using automated programs or services to create links to your site.

allClaims.claim: PBNs / link farms are categorized by Google as link schemes and are detected at network level by SpamBrain; consequences range from algorithmic devaluation to manual action to de-indexation. King Maker excludes PBNs entirely — the downside (whole-site removal) is uninsurable against an organic-dominance offer.
allClaims.stat: Penalty range: link devaluation → manual action → complete removal from search results
allClaims.snippet: Any links intended to manipulate rankings in Google Search results may be considered link spam. This includes any behavior that manipulates links to your site or outgoing links from your site.

allClaims.claim: Scholarship link building is a documented penalty line — Google cited a scholarship-link page among the example URLs in a real manual-action notice. King Maker explicitly EXCLUDES scholarship links. Caveat: the cited author notes the scholarship link may have been incidental to other paid-link violations rather than the sole trigger, so treat it as a 'do not touch' boundary rather than a guaranteed-penalty mechanism.
allClaims.stat: First documented manual action explicitly listing a scholarship link page among example unnatural-link URLs (2021)
allClaims.snippet: When Google provided examples of unnatural links in their manual action notice... two of those were guest blog posts, and the third example URL was a scholarship link page. It's possible that the paid links were what flagged the site for the manual action and that the guest post and scholarship links were already being ignored but were called out as manipulative as an example.

allClaims.claim: The single highest-ROI one-time GBP-optimization lever is the PRIMARY CATEGORY — it is the #1 local-pack ranking factor per the 2026 Local Search Ranking Factors survey, defines the competitor set the business is judged against, and acts as a strict relevance filter. A shippable GBP asset kit that nails primary category + ~4 secondary categories is a genuine one-time off-page deliverable.
allClaims.stat: Primary GBP category = #1 local-pack factor; businesses using ~4 additional categories average map position 5.9 (additional categories = 8th-ranked factor)
allClaims.snippet: Primary GBP category is listed as the top local pack ranking factor... Selecting the appropriate primary category for your business is crucial for local search rankings... businesses using four additional categories within their GBPs have the highest average map ranking of 5.9.

allClaims.claim: Whitespark independently corroborates the primary-category lever: choosing the wrong primary category is the second most common reason businesses rank poorly. Pick the most specific category matching the core service. This is the cheapest, highest-leverage one-time fix in the GBP asset kit.
allClaims.stat: Wrong primary category = #2 most common cause of poor local ranking
allClaims.snippet: Choosing the wrong primary category is the second most common reason businesses rank poorly. Your primary category tells Google exactly what your business does — a plumber listed as 'contractor' instead of 'plumber' will lose to actual plumbers every time.

allClaims.claim: IMPORTANT NUANCE for the GBP asset kit: photos and Google Posts do NOT meaningfully move LOCAL-PACK RANKING per the 2026 survey (geo-tagged photos = little impact; quantity of posts = no ranking influence). Sell photo/post assets as CONVERSION and freshness levers, not as ranking levers — overselling them as a ranking factor is a defensibility miss.
allClaims.stat: Geo-tagged photos: little ranking impact; quantity of Google posts: no ranking influence (2026 LSRF)
allClaims.snippet: Geo-tagged photos uploaded to GBP have little impact... Quantity of Google posts/updates does not influence rankings.

allClaims.claim: Where GBP photos DO pay off is conversion/engagement, and that justifies a one-time photo-kit asset. Google's own first-party data: profiles with photos get 42% more direction requests and 35% more website click-throughs than those without. (The 100+ photos / 520% calls figures circulating online are correlational and not first-party — do not cite those.)
allClaims.stat: Google first-party: +42% direction requests, +35% website clicks for profiles with photos vs none
allClaims.snippet: Businesses with photos receive 42% more requests for driving directions and 35% more clicks through to their websites than businesses that don't have photos.

allClaims.claim: Reactive digital PR / expert-commentary newsjacking (HARO's successor) is a high-ceiling, white-hat, one-time-shippable lever: King Maker ships the ASSET (a pre-built expert-bio, topic-angle, pitch-template kit + monitoring setup), and the resulting link is fully editorial — the journalist reaches out, zero manipulation. Promise the asset (the FLOOR); the link itself is EARNED, never guaranteed (the CEILING).
allClaims.stat: HARO permanently closed Dec 9 2024; relaunched under Featured.com Apr 22 2025; Qwoted/Featured/Connectively are the active journalist-sourcing platforms
allClaims.snippet: Connectively (the new version of HARO) was permanently closed on December 9, 2024... On April 22, 2025, HARO officially relaunched under Featured.com... Connectively (formerly HARO), Qwoted, and Featured.com connect experts with journalists actively seeking quotes.

allClaims.claim: Reactive expert commentary is recognized as one of the three highest-performing white-hat digital-PR formats, and a well-timed expert quote often earns more links than a planned campaign at a fraction of the effort — and it is purely editorial-driven, so it sits cleanly on the safe side of Google's link-spam line.
allClaims.stat: Three top digital-PR formats: original data studies, reactive expert commentary (newsjacking), free tools/calculators
allClaims.snippet: The three highest-performing digital PR formats are: original data studies, expert reactive commentary (newsjacking), and free tools or calculators... a well-timed expert quote in a major publication often earns more links than a planned campaign at a fraction of the effort.

allClaims.claim: Local sponsorship + chamber-of-commerce / local-event listings are a legitimate white-hat, one-time-shippable link lever: sponsoring a local event or joining the chamber produces a listing/link on their site, and these are explicitly framed as white-hat local link-building (topically/geographically relevant). King Maker ships the target-list + outreach-template asset; the link is earned via a real sponsorship, NOT bought as a ranking link with optimized anchors.
allClaims.stat: Chamber/event/school links cited as valuable, white-hat local-SEO links
allClaims.snippet: A link from a local chamber of commerce, event, or school can be valuable for local SEO, and sponsoring a local event can result in being listed on their website as a white hat link-building strategy.

allClaims.claim: For roofers specifically, the highest-relevance one-time link is the manufacturer find-a-pro listing (GAF Master Elite, Owens Corning Platinum Preferred, CertainTeed SELECT ShingleMaster). These are credential-gated, high-authority, topically perfect directories the client is already eligible for via certification — a true one-time setup asset, not a purchased link.
allClaims.stat: All three majors (GAF/OC/CertainTeed) run public Find-a-Contractor locators with tiered certification gates
allClaims.snippet: You can look up companies directly on the manufacturer's sites using the GAF contractor locator, Owens Corning locator, and CertainTeed locator. If the company isn't listed, the certification isn't current.

allClaims.claim: Reviews are the strongest CLIENT-CONTROLLABLE one-time-plus-velocity lever after the GBP profile itself: review weight rose from 16% (2023) to 20% (2026), making them the #2 local-pack factor after primary category, and responding to 80%+ of reviews shows a measurable ranking boost. A one-time review-system + response-template asset is shippable; the ongoing velocity is the client's job (out of one-time scope, noted not centered).
allClaims.stat: Review weight 16% (2023) → 20% (2026); 80%+ response rate = measurable ranking boost
allClaims.snippet: Review signals are one of the strongest ranking factors you can control, accounting for 16-20% of local ranking weight... Businesses that respond to 80% or more of reviews see a measurable ranking boost.

allClaims.claim: All of these one-time off-page levers move the ORGANIC engine more than the pack, which keeps King Maker's spine intact: on-page is ~19% of controllable local factors and rising, with localized location pages + strong internal linking central. verdicts.claim: Internal links convert to traffic up to a sweet spot, then reverse: a 23-million-internal-link study found URLs with 0-4 internal links averaged ~2 clicks vs ~4x for 40-44 links, after which traffic declines past ~45-50 links. (2) The NichePursuits interview transcript has Cyrus saying the curve "zigzags up and down" after roughly 20-30 links and that ANCHOR-TEXT VARIETY — not raw link count — is the dominant traffic driver; the clean 45-50 reversal point is the aggregate-bucket framing, and the real driver is varied unique (non-navigational) links, not link volume per se. The decline past 45-50 is attributed to sitewide/navigation links pointing at low-value URLs, an artifact of nav structure rather than a penalty for "too many links."

verdicts.claim: GBP photos/posts do NOT move local-pack ranking per the 2026 survey — they are a CONVERSION lever. Google's first-party data: profiles with photos get +42% direction requests and +35% website clicks vs none.

The numeric figures ARE corroborated independently: Whitespark's GBP photos guide states verbatim "42% more requests for directions and 35% more website URL clicks (citing Google data)," and the same 42%/35% pairing recurs across many independent local-SEO sources, all attributing it to Google. On the ranking question, Whitespark's Local Search Ranking Factors classifies GBP Photos as a CONVERSION factor (supports the claim), but multiple 2026 sources flag an emerging INDIRECT ranking pathway via Google Vision AI image analysis and AI-Overview inclusion.
verdicts.counterEvidence: Two bounding issues. (1) Citation mismatch: the cited brightlocal.com/learn/.../photos/ page does NOT contain the 42%/35% figures — it carries only Google's non-numeric phrasing, and it does NOT support the sub-stats "geo-tagged photos: little ranking impact" or "post quantity: no ranking influence" (the page neither asserts geo-tag ranking impact nor addresses post-quantity ranking at all). (2) The absolute "photos do NOT move local-pack ranking" is overstated for 2026: Whitespark and several 2026 guides note Google Vision AI now reads image content as a relevance signal and image quality gates AI-Overview/AI-card inclusion — an indirect ranking influence that the flat "do NOT move ranking" wording ignores. The 42%/35% are also Google self-reported engagement correlations, not a controlled causal study (selection bias: engaged owners who add photos also do other things).
verdicts.reasoning: The claim splits into a verifiable stat and an analytical framing. The STAT (photos: +42% direction requests, +35% website clicks, Google first-party) is well-corroborated and the numbers are accurate — Whitespark cites them verbatim to Google and the pairing is local-SEO canon — so no correction of the figures is warranted (rules out 'corrected'/'killed'). The FRAMING (conversion lever, not a ranking lever) is directionally supported by Whitespark's Local Search Ranking Factors classifying photos as a conversion factor. Two defects keep it from 'survived': (a) the cited BrightLocal URL is the wrong source for the 42%/35% numbers — it only carries Google's qualitative version, and it does not support the two ranking sub-stats at all, so the citation is mis-attributed; (b) the unqualified "do NOT move ranking" is too absolute for 2026, where Vision AI image-content relevance and AI-Overview image-quality gating create an indirect ranking pathway. Recommended fixes: re-cite the 42%/35% to Whitespark's GBP photos guide (or Google's own GBP help/engagement docs) rather than the BrightLocal optimization page; and soften to "photos are primarily a CONVERSION lever and are not a traditional local-pack ranking factor, though in 2026 they feed indirect relevance via Vision AI / AI-Overview inclusion." Survives as the substance is real; flagged because the citation and the absolutism need repair.

thesis.confidence: High on the MECHANISM and DIRECTION; Medium on the MAGNITUDES. Why: the thesis's structural spine is carried by measured, primary, independent evidence — the pack's proximity cap (Vicinity update, Sterling Sky; rankings.io geo-grid: -8 positions per mile, n=1,100 firms x 225 grid points), and organic's scale lever (Ahrefs n=324,522 page-count-to-traffic; SearchPilot controlled split-test +25% organic from internal linking). Those survive cleanly. What caps it below STRONGLY SUPPORTED: the load-bearing 57%-organic / 52%-pack weight split is MODELED — a Whitespark 2026 expert-opinion survey (~47 practitioners scoring 187 factors), explicitly not Google-published coefficients (digest flags this itself). The single largest MEASURED pack study (Sterling Sky, n=8,186 / 200 cities) finds only a "slight correlation" for on-page content in the pack and shows review-recency + visible address dominating — which is consistent with the thesis (it routes organic AWAY from the pack) but caps how hard "organic feeds the pack" can be pushed. Net: defensible as a directional, ranges-based offer thesis; not defensible as a precise-percentage promise.
thesis.floorCeiling: HONEST INFILTRATION SHAPE (both curves MODELED — claim the SHAPE and ranges, NEVER a job count; "jobs/week" is snake oil). PACK: a proximity-fractured, review-gated "Christmas tree" — green near the office, red across the rest of the radius (rankings.io: ~-8 positions in the first mile; Sterling Sky 2:1 triangle clustering holds even in LA/Houston-scale metros). Early it contributes on the order of ~1-2 jobs/MONTH because it is doubly gated: proximity (~5-7mi structural cap, post-Vicinity) AND review velocity (Sterling Sky: rankings fall off after ~18 days without a new review). It matures toward an upper band of ~10/mo only near a ~2-year ceiling, after review count/velocity and GBP signals compound. ORGANIC: carries months ~1-18 — no proximity-grid penalty, and it harvests the zero-pack long-tail (informational + non-"near me" queries the pack never shows for). This is where regional dominance and the path past a 5-7mi radius actually live; it is also the only lever that can absorb a $5-10k/mo off-page budget without tripping spam flags. Promise the FLOOR (the shape: organic-led months 1-18, pack as a slow proximity-capped byproduct), project the CEILING (pack ~10/mo at ~2yr) — and never convert either into a per-week or guaranteed job number.
conditions: Sustained ~$5-10k/mo OFF-PAGE investment is required for the organic-dominance engine to clear a 5-7mi radius and scale toward $5-10M — only an enterprise/deep site can absorb that spend without thin-site over-optimization spam flags (Google: unnatural links are devalued by default, with manual-action/Penguin demotion as the tail risk). NOTE: ongoing client-managed off-page is out of scope for what King Maker ships; this condition is a market reality stated, not a deliverable.

An UNSCREENED, single write-review link routing EVERY customer is mandatory — review gating (satisfaction pre-screening that routes only happy customers) violates Google policy AND the FTC final rule effective Oct 21, 2024, with civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation (2026). The pack byproduct depends on review velocity (the fastest pack lever), so the machine must drive volume without gating.
honestyCorrections: LEAD-QUALITY / 'organic out-clicks the pack' is HIGH-TICKET-SCOPED and intent-split, NOT a blanket win. The only controlled click study (BrightLocal, n=5,500) showing organic ~44-51% vs pack ~29-32% is FLAGGED Medium and explicitly counters that the pack carries higher trust (~68% vs 27%) and wins the high-intent slice. Separately, the 2025 aggregate click-share reality is pack ~44% > organic ~29% > paid ~19%. So the organic case is SCALE + CONTROL + research/consideration-stage capture (where high-ticket roofing buyers actually live), not raw click-share — never claim organic beats the pack for clicks in general.

The 57%-organic / 52%-pack weight split is MODELED expert-survey opinion (Whitespark 2026, ~47 practitioners, NOT Google data) — present it as a directional rank (+/- several points), never as measured Google coefficients. The corroborating MEASURED study (Sterling Sky n=8,186) finds only a 'slight' on-page correlation inside the pack.

The 'pre-sold authority' / consideration-stage conversion framing (e.g. ~70% pre-sold, 60-70% click-skip-past-ads) is MODELED / claim-library, not in the verified digest — label it directional and do not cite it as measured.

The roofing manufacturer-locator backlink (GAF/OC/CertainTeed 'find a contractor') is the highest-leverage one-time off-page win on RELEVANCE/trust/AI-citation grounds, but it is UNVERIFIED whether those listings pass dofollow link equity this session — pitch it as a relevance/AI-citation signal, not a confirmed equity backlink, until per-manufacturer HTML is inspected. Also: credential gate %s (GAF ~2-3%, OC/CertainTeed <1%) are manufacturer-published marketing, not third-party audited.
thesis.bottomLine: SUPPORTED, defensibly. For high-ticket roofing, leading with ORGANIC regional dominance as the engine and the offer headline is the correct, evidence-backed frame — and centering the map pack would be wrong. The pack is structurally proximity-capped (~5-7mi; Vicinity update + measured -8 ranking positions per first mile) and doubly gated by proximity AND review velocity/GBP, so it cannot scale to $5-10M off a 5-7mi radius and arrives as a slow byproduct (modeled ~1-2 jobs/mo early, maturing toward ~10/mo only near a ~2yr ceiling). Organic carries months ~1-18, faces no proximity-grid penalty, harvests the zero-pack long-tail, and is the only lever that can absorb a $5-10k/mo budget without tripping spam flags — backed by measured scale data (Ahrefs n=324,522) and a controlled +25% internal-linking split-test. Three guardrails keep it bulletproof and FTC-safe: (1) the ranking-weight percentages are MODELED expert-survey, not Google data — claim them as directional ranges, never coefficients; (2) the lead-quality/'organic out-clicks pack' claim is intent-split and high-ticket-scoped, not a blanket click-share win (2025 reality: pack 44% > organic 29%); (3) reviews must route unscreened (FTC rule, up to $53,088/violation) and no PBNs/link schemes, ever. Promise the shape and the floor; project the ceiling; never quote a job count.

guardrails.ftcPosture: King Maker's organic-dominance offer is sold in RANGES, never point-promises: we promise the floor and project the ceiling, and we label every number as measured, modeled, or directional. The competitive claim is organic regional dominance — a deep, genuinely-unique site plus one-time shippable off-page (GBP primary-category fix, the 30-50 foundational citations, the GBP-link-to-dedicated-landing pattern, a manufacturer-locator listing where the contractor already qualifies, and a one-time reactive-digital-PR asset). The map pack is a proximity-capped (~5-7mi, hard structural gate per the Vicinity update and the -8-positions-per-first-mile geo-grid data) BYPRODUCT we deliver, not the headline. We NEVER use PBNs, paid links, link exchanges, optimized-anchor schemes, or any tactic Google's first-party spam policy names — those risk devaluation at best and removal-from-search at worst, and we exclude them by name. We NEVER gate reviews: satisfaction pre-screening that routes only happy customers to Google violates both Google policy and the FTC's final Rule on fake/deceptive reviews (effective Oct 21, 2024; civil penalties up to $53,088 per violation in 2026), so the review machine routes every customer to one unscreened write-review link. We do not claim certifications we do not hold (no SOC 2, no bank-level, no HIPAA); we position on verifiable ACTIONS we actually take and can show — schema/sameAs entity clarity, OWASP-style hardening, a consistent shown NAP, internal-link architecture (a controlled split-test measured a 25% organic uplift), and rankable page depth (median organic traffic scales with rankable page count across 324,522 sites). Because the percentages we cite are largely a Whitespark expert-opinion survey (47 experts, 187 factors — modeled, not Google-published), we present them as directional ranks plus or minus several points and corroborate with independent measured studies (Sterling Sky's 8,186-business/200-city analysis) wherever a number is load-bearing. Polished false confidence is the cardinal sin; the floor is always honest.
neverClaim: You win the local map pack by building more/deeper pages — pages are an organic-rank lever (on-page ~33% + links ~24% of organic), but the pack is dominated by GBP (~32%) + reviews (~20%) and proximity; on-page is only ~15% and links only ~8% of pack weight (Whitespark 2026, modeled).

Proximity is '55%' (or any single precise %) of local ranking — the digest carries NO measured miles-per-rank or proximity-percentage figure; proximity is a hard structural gate stated mechanistically/directionally, not a clean coefficient.

A point-promise jobs-per-week / leads-per-month number — no source supports a guaranteed lead or job volume; click-share is ~44% pack / ~29% organic in 2025 (directional, secondhand), which sizes opportunity, not a per-client yield.

'Guaranteed rankings' / 'guaranteed top-3' — rankings are influenced by factors we do not control (proximity, competitor velocity, Google updates); guarantees must be redefined in organic money-terms with a floor, never a pack-position promise.

Any use of PBNs, bought/sold links, link exchanges, paid advertorials, automated links, or optimized money-keyword anchor schemes — Google's first-party spam policy names these and penalizes up to complete removal from search; King Maker excludes them entirely.

'We own/manage your Yext listings' or selling Yext-as-owned recurring syndication — citations are a one-time top-30-50 foundation with no recurring fees under ~100 locations; do not frame an ongoing paid listing-syndication subscription as part of the build.

Self-hosted/embedded reviews marked up with our own schema will show Google star rich-results — self-controlled review markup is INELIGIBLE for the star feature; the on-site widget is a content/E-E-A-T/conversion asset, not a SERP-star play.

SOC 2 / bank-level / HIPAA / 'compliant' / 'certified' security — never claim attestations we don't hold; the FTC enforces false security claims independent of any breach. Position on actions (OWASP-hardened, zero-stored-data).

Confirmed dofollow link equity from GAF/Owens Corning/CertainTeed locator listings — NOT verified this session; treat manufacturer locators as relevance/trust/AI-citation signals until per-manufacturer HTML is inspected, not as confirmed backlinks.

Schema markup gets you '28-40% more AI citations' or otherwise drives rankings/AI-citation rate — an independent Dec-2024 study found NO correlation; schema is eligibility/extraction infrastructure, not a ranking or citation driver.

'Organic beats the pack' as a blanket statement — the controlled click study splits by INTENT: organic out-clicks on volume (~44-51% vs ~29-32%) but the pack carries higher trust (~68%) and wins the high-intent slice.

A thin/competitor site will get penalized/collapse from over-optimization — the enforcement default is link DEVALUATION (wasted budget), not a guaranteed penalty; sell our efficiency and safety, not a competitor's collapse.
GBP photos/posts improve pack ranking — they do NOT move ranking per the 2026 survey; they are a conversion lever (Google first-party: +42% direction requests, +35% website clicks).
A digital-PR or HARO-successor link is guaranteed — reactive digital PR ships as a one-time asset (bio + angles + pitch templates); the resulting link is editorial and earned, never guaranteed.

We guarantee the work and the organic-prominence floor, defined in money-terms, not a pack position we can't promise — proximity, competitor review velocity, and Google updates are outside any vendor's control.
